The backlash resulted in Macklemore being dropped from the inaugural Neon City Festival in Las Vegas, Nevada.
One week after Macklemore repeatedly called to "Free Palestine" and performed "Hind’s Hall" while opening for Sheeran, the rapper was dropped from the remaining U.S. dates.

title: Richard Branson’s wife could have survived with crucial medication, coroner finds
summary: A British coroner found Lady Joan Branson's fatal pulmonary embolism could have been prevented with blood thinners after her fall on Necker Island.
story: NASCAR driver Kyle Busch, 41, tragically died from severe pneumonia that escalated into sepsis, his family confirmed. Dr. Cedric Rutland, a pulmonary critical care physician and American Lung Association spokesperson, explains how pneumonia's inflammation and infection can overwhelm the body.
The death of Richard Branson's wife, Lady Joan Branson, could have been prevented if she had received medication to prevent blood clots, a British coroner reportedly found.
Lady Branson died at 80 after being admitted to the hospital in November 2025 after a fall weeks earlier on Necker Island, a British Virgin Island owned by her billionaire husband.
Her cause of death was determined to be a pulmonary embolism caused by deep vein thrombosis (DVT), in which a blood clot travels to the lungs and blocks an artery, the BBC reported.
KIM KARDASHIAN REVEALS NEW HEALTH SCARE WITH HAUNTING CONNECTION TO FATHER'S CANCER DEATH

Senior coroner Fiona Wilcox told Westminster Coroner's Court earlier this month that Lady Branson did not receive preventive anticoagulants, commonly known as blood thinners, at the hospital despite a "very high risk of developing deep vein thrombosis," according to the outlet.
A British coroner concluded Lady Joan Branson's death likely could have been prevented with preventive blood-thinning medication. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)
According to testimony during the legal inquest, Lady Branson's biggest risk factors included her immobility after a fracture following her fall.
"I do find her death would have likely been prevented and the lack of anticoagulation did cause or contribute to her death probably," Wilcox said.
COMMON ANTIBIOTIC LINKED TO HIGHER RISK OF DEATH IN ADULTS, MAJOR STUDY FINDS
Wilcox added, however, that the case was not one of neglect because Branson did receive medical care.
The inquest, she said, was to "explore the facts, come to the correct conclusions and learn lessons from this," The Independent reported.
The inquest into Lady Joan Branson's death has drawn attention to the importance of preventing dangerous blood clots in hospitalized patients. (Tim Graham/Sygma/Corbis via Getty Images))

During the inquest, doctors gave differing testimony about whether bleeding risk justified withholding the medication, namely enoxaparin, an injectable blood thinner commonly used to help prevent blood clots in hospitalized patients.
EVERYDAY HABIT LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DYING FROM HEART DISEASE
The hospital's admitting doctor, Dr. Basir Kunduzi, testified that he did not complete a bleeding risk assessment on the day of Lady Branson's admission.
Kunduzi said Lady Branson's death led him to "reflect on [his] role as a doctor" and the importance of "good communication between team members," according to the BBC.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Fox News Digital has reached out to the hospital for comment.
The case highlights the importance of balancing blood clot prevention with bleeding risk when treating hospitalized patients. (iStock)

The findings highlight the lifesaving role of blood thinners, which are often used in hospitals to help prevent DVT in patients who are unable to move normally after surgery, fractures or prolonged bed rest. They can increase the risk of bleeding, however, so doctors must weigh both risks before giving them.

Nearly all hospitalized adults should receive some form of blood clot prevention, either with blood-thinning medication or mechanical devices that help keep blood flowing in the legs, Dr. Jared Ross, a South Carolina-based emergency medicine physician, told Fox News Digital.
"In the vast majority of cases, the benefits outweigh the risks," Ross, who was not involved in the inquest or Branson's care, added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
A spokeswoman for Sir Branson said the family does not plan to comment on the inquest and pointed to the numerous social media posts he has made for his wife.
Sir Richard Branson paid tribute to his wife after her death, calling her the "shining star" of their family. (Photo by Patrick T. FALLON / AFP) (Photo by PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images)

"Life will never be the same without her," Branson wrote on Instagram last year, calling her the "shining star" of the family. "But we have fifty incredible years of memories — years filled with tears and laughter, kindness, and a love that shaped our family more than words could ever capture. It was a relationship that worked. We just had lots of laughs. We were very lucky."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
Although pulmonary embolisms can be life-threatening, prompt treatment greatly improves the chances of survival, making early recognition critical.
Symptoms of DVT can include swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth and redness in the affected leg or arm, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Richard Branson and Joan Templeman married on Necker Island in 1989 — the same private Caribbean island where she suffered the fall that preceded her final hospitalization. (PA Images via Getty Images)

A pulmonary embolism, which occurs when a clot travels to the lungs, may cause shortness of breath, chest pain that worsens with deep breathing or coughing, a rapid or irregular heartbeat, coughing up blood, lightheadedness or fainting.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The CDC and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute say anyone with symptoms of a pulmonary embolism should seek immediate medical attention.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Tropical disease spread by mosquitoes claims first recorded death in southern US state
summary: Gay Small died on her 80th birthday from dengue after a mosquito bite near her Tampa home, the Florida Department of Health confirmed Friday.
story: Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious diseases and addiction medicine doctor and associate professor at University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine, discusses the spread, symptoms and management of West Nile virus.
Florida recorded its first confirmed dengue fever death of 2026 earlier this month, according to the Florida Department of Health.

Gay Small of Hillsborough County died on Sept. 4 — her 80th birthday — from complications of a dengue infection, including septic shock and multi-organ failure, after she was bitten by a mosquito near her home on Bayshore Boulevard, the Tampa Bay Times reported.

"Cheated, just, you know, it’s so unfair because she was in good health, and she worked hard to stay healthy, and she walked, and she ate right and you know, all the things that you’re supposed to do," Small's daughter, Anna Small, told Tampa's WFLA Channel 8.
DANGEROUS MOSQUITO-BORNE VIRUS SPREADS IN ONE STATE AS OFFICIALS WARN OF RISING CASES
"And you know, this virus just kind of comes out of nowhere. She met the wrong mosquito, and that’s it," Anna Small said.
Small's family said they believe Gay Small first caught dengue years ago while traveling abroad but didn't know it. People who have had dengue before are much more likely to develop severe symptoms.

"While in the hospital, Small said her mother was weak, her hands turned red, and she had trembles that she could hear in her voice," reported WFLA. "She had to go into the ICU by the middle of the week."
A mosquito feeds on human skin. Dengue is spread to people through the bite of an infected mosquito and can cause fever, severe aches, nausea and rash. (iStock)
Small's late husband, Bob Small, spent his career working on dengue vaccines, according to the couple's daughter.
The Florida Department of Health confirmed the death Friday after completing its investigation, but did not release additional information, WFLA reported.
The Times, citing University of South Florida public-health instructor Kristi Miley, reported that a dengue death had not been recorded in the Tampa Bay area in nearly a century.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The virus is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas.

Florida mosquito-control agencies have stepped up surveillance, inspections and spraying, as locally acquired dengue fever cases — which means people contracted the illness where they live rather than while traveling abroad — have climbed in recent weeks.
Gay Small’s late husband, Bob Small, spent his career working on dengue vaccines — the same mosquito-borne disease that ultimately claimed his wife’s life, according to reports. (iStock)

The Times reported that since July, Florida "has been experiencing an unprecedented outbreak of locally caught cases." Hillsborough County, where Small lived, "has been at the epicenter of the epidemic."
Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts issued by the Florida Department of Health.
"Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro told Fox 13.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
"The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day," he said.

"When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission."

In addition to increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services has also been inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to local reports.
Mosquito-control crews across the Tampa Bay area have increased surveillance and treatments as locally acquired dengue cases climb. (iStock)

The increased application of insecticide and larvicide by helicopters appears to be working, the Times reported, as, "Of the last 1,500 mosquitoes they've sent for testing, all have returned negative for dengue."

The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) is urging residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say.
The FMCA also advises people to follow what it calls the "three Ds."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.Defend with a repellent containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus.Dump standing water from containers around the home, and check yards regularly.
Dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.
Defend with a repellent containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus.
Dump standing water from containers around the home, and check yards regularly.

Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic. In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness. People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.

title: Women turn to testosterone for low sex drive as doctors confront treatment ‘experimentation’
summary: Dr. Kudzai Dombo reveals the insurance denials and dosing guesswork women face seeking testosterone therapy as FDA regulators weigh new access.
story: OB-GYN Dr. Kudzai Dombo shares why interest in testosterone is rising among women, what evidence says about libido, and why access, dosing and insurance coverage can be complicated.

When women ask their doctors about taking testosterone to help with menopause symptoms, they can run into insurance rejections, confusing workarounds and dosing guesswork, as no testosterone product is FDA-approved for women in the U.S.
On Thursday, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) convened a public workshop to examine the evidence, safety and research gaps surrounding testosterone therapy for menopausal women.

Interest in testosterone therapy has grown as more women seek treatment for symptoms such as low sexual desire, fatigue and reduced quality of life during menopause — yet the lack of an FDA-approved product has left physicians relying on off-label prescribing and compounded formulations.
MELINDA FRENCH GATES SAYS IT TOOK 3 DOCTORS TO DIAGNOSE THE CONDITION SHE WAS SUFFERING FROM

Dr. Kudzai Dombo, a board-certified obstetrician-gynecologist, Menopause Society-certified practitioner, and prescribing physician at Alloy Health, said she sees this dynamic playing out daily in her own Los Angeles practice.
Interest in testosterone therapy has grown as more women seek treatment for symptoms such as low sexual desire, fatigue and reduced quality of life during menopause, doctors say. (iStock)
Once patients get settled on standard estrogen and progesterone regimens, "The immediate next question is, do I need testosterone?" Dombo told Fox News Digital.

Although women may hear about a wide range of potential benefits on social media and from friends, current evidence-based guidelines support testosterone therapy for only one indication: hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD), or persistently low sexual desire.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Clinical evidence supporting its use for energy, mood, bone health or sleep remains limited — though many patients are eager to try it for those secondary benefits, according to Dombo.
The absence of FDA-approved female testosterone products forces patients to rely on compounded creams, over-the-counter purchases abroad or micro-dosed male gels. (iStock)

Because no female-specific formulation exists, doctors must navigate off-label workarounds. They typically choose between using custom compounding pharmacies or micro-dosing FDA-approved male gel packets, which patients must carefully measure out at home.
ALZHEIMER'S RISK MAY BE 35% LOWER WITH COMMON MENOPAUSE TREATMENT, STUDY FINDS

This lack of standardized options creates administrative and financial hurdles. Because the therapy is off-label, insurance routinely denies coverage, forcing clinicians and patients to improvise — a frustration that Dombo experienced firsthand.

"When I was prescribed testosterone, my insurance denied coverage, and my physician recommended a compounded cream to avoid the administrative burden," Dombo recalled. "I said, 'Well, I've already tried compounded and I actually want to try the gel.'"
"Sexual health is part of your entire health."
Using a discount coupon, she paid out of pocket and discovered that a 10-month supply of male gel packets was actually cheaper than a single month of compounded cream.
"It's just an example, I think, of how we have to adapt to a system that has not supported patients when it comes to access to testosterone therapy," she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Dosing male products can also present clinical challenges. Dombo described a patient in her private practice who precisely measured out one-tenth of a male gel packet daily using a syringe.
Despite three months of consistency, follow-up bloodwork showed no change in hormone levels, and the patient experienced no symptom relief.
Rising advocacy from patients and medical professionals has pushed federal regulators to officially evaluate standardized access and scientific evidence for female testosterone therapy. (iStock)

"We're left to kind of decide, 'Well, what now?'" Dombo said. "It's all experimentation ... We don't have a set guideline for how to be able to do this for women. We have to rely on the art of medicine."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The latest federal meeting represents a critical step forward, according to Dombo, who believes grassroots advocacy from patients and clinicians is forcing regulatory action.
"We're not going to stop knocking on the door, because there are several of us who believe that women deserve to be able to have access to just what they need," she said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Sexual health is part of your entire health," Dombo emphasized, expressing optimism that regulatory agencies will eventually adapt to support safer, standardized access.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Kim Kardashian reveals new health scare with haunting connection to father’s cancer death
summary: Kim Kardashian reveals her esophagitis diagnosis in a new "Kardashians" trailer, raising fears tied to her father's esophageal cancer death.
story: Dr. Brian M. Slomovitz, director of gynecologic oncology at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida, says ovarian cancer was once known as the ‘silent killer,’ meaning it was often undetected until it reached an advanced stage.
Kim Kardashian is opening up about a new health diagnosis that hits close to home.
In a new trailer for "The Kardashians," the reality star, 45, revealed that she has esophagitis, which is inflammation of the esophagus.
The diagnosis held a particular significance given that her father, Robert Kardashian Sr., died of esophageal cancer in 2003 at age 59.
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND
In the episode, the Skims founder is seen lying on a hospital bed as someone off camera asks, "Didn’t your father ... isn’t it what he died of?"
In a new trailer for "The Kardashians," Kim Kardashian revealed she has esophagitis, which is inflammation of the esophagus. (Getty Images)
Kardashian’s manager and mother, Kris Jenner, became emotional at this suggestion, saying, "I can’t. It makes me want to cry."
Experts have noted, however, that the two conditions are not the same.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Kim Kardashian's diagnosis, esophagitis, is an inflammation of the esophagus, the muscular tube that carries food from the throat to the stomach. It is most commonly caused by acid reflux, certain medications, infections or allergies, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK).
The diagnosis held a particular significance given that her father, Robert Kardashian Sr., died of esophageal cancer in 2003 at age 59. (Getty Images)

Esophageal cancer occurs when malignant cells form in the tissues lining the esophagus, according to the National Cancer Institute. There are two main types: squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma.

While esophagitis itself does not directly cause cancer, the chronic inflammation can in some cases lead to Barrett's esophagus, a precancerous condition that can increase the higher risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma. This risk is higher among those with ongoing acid reflux (GERD).
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
About 5% to 15% of people with GERD develop Barrett's esophagus, although most people with Barrett's do not develop esophageal cancer, the NIDDK states.
Robert Kardashian and daughter Kim Kardashian stand outside of her private high school, Marymount High School, in Los Angeles, in 1996. (Getty Images)
For those who have been diagnosed with esophagitis, the Mayo Clinic provides the following recommendations to manage symptoms and reduce future cancer risk.

Avoid foods and drinks that may worsen reflux, including alcohol, caffeine, chocolate and mint.
Wait at least three hours after eating before lying down and stay elevated if nighttime reflux is an issue.
Lose excess weight and quit smoking, if applicable, to help reduce reflux and promote healing.
Follow up with a gastroenterologist if symptoms persist or if complications develop.
In another health scare, Kardashian revealed in 2025 that her doctors discovered a small, unruptured brain aneurysm during an MRI scan. (Getty Images)

"They’re like, 'It’s been there for, like, years. It was here a few years ago,’" she said in an episode of "The Kardashians."

title: Celebrity plastic surgeon reveals when it's too soon for a facelift, and when waiting can backfire
summary: Dr. Terry Dubrow reveals why Kris Jenner's public facelift is driving 38-year-olds to seek facelift surgery they don't yet need.
story: During an episode of Josh Peck’s podcast, "Good Guys," the Beverly Hills plastic surgeon weighs in on growing demand for cosmetic procedures among younger adults and explains why patients with early skin laxity may be better served by waiting.
When it comes to getting a facelift, timing may be everything.
Going under the knife too soon could mean having surgery before it’s necessary — but waiting too long can also backfire, according to celebrity plastic surgeon Dr. Terry Dubrow.
During an episode of Josh Peck’s and Ben Soffer's podcast, "Good Guys," the Beverly Hills-based surgeon said some women are jumping the gun and getting the procedure too soon.
CHEAP SURGERY OVERSEAS MAY COME WITH DEVASTATING COMPLICATIONS, DOCTORS WARN
"For those people in their 30s who want some skin tightening, they need to wait, 'cause there will be the technology that will allow early facelifts without cutting," he said.
Dubrow also mentioned Kris Jenner’s recent facelift, which may have motivated women to seek out the procedure based on her results.
Going under the knife too soon could mean having surgery before it’s necessary — but waiting too long can also backfire, according to a celebrity plastic surgeon. (iStock)
"That made facelifts like, ‘Oh, Kris Jenner did it and made it public. Now it's cool. Everybody get a facelift,’" he said.

"So then you're seeing 38-year-old people in your office wanting a facelift, and you go, ‘OK, hold on a second. You don't even need a facelift. You need to wait, because, you know, a facelift is incisions and scars, and elevating up the skin, numbness and all sorts of potential things that can go wrong."
MEN FACE NEW PRESSURE TO STAY ‘HOT’ AS THEY AGE — AND IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT LIVING LONGER
Dubrow warned that if people have too many facelifts, "when it starts to relax, it can relax in weird ways."
"You've all seen it — people who look pretty good, but there's something about the way their skin lies on their face that looks unnatural, and it ruins the whole look," he warned.
Dr. Terry Dubrow warned that if people have too many facelifts, "when it starts to relax, it can relax in weird ways." (Getty Images)
"If you have early laxity, don't go in for your ‘Kris Jenner facelift.’ Still wait, because that technology is just around the corner."

Conversely, the surgeon has warned that waiting too long — while relying on other nonsurgical fixes — can also backfire. "A lot of women are staying on the ‘nonsurgical treadmill’ for too long," Dubrow told Fox News Digital.
DO RED LIGHT THERAPY AND COLD PLUNGES REALLY WORK? A DOCTOR REVEALS THE TRUTH
"They keep adding filler, lasers and tightening treatments, when the real problem is that the deeper tissues have dropped."

While it is possible to get a great result with a later-in-life facelift, the doctor pointed out that as the skin becomes looser, the tissues descend further, which may require more extensive surgery.

While it is possible to get a great result with a later-in-life facelift, the doctor pointed out that as the skin becomes looser, the tissues descend further, which may require more extensive surgery. (iStock)
"My feeling is that once those treatments stop producing a natural result, continuing to postpone surgery can actually make you look less natural."
That’s not to say that nonsurgical treatments don’t have their place, he noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Fillers, lasers and tightening treatments can buy you time when they are used intelligently — but fillers cannot lift sagging tissue, and too much filler can make someone look distorted."
"The right time should be based on your face, not the doctor’s menu."

Aggressive energy treatments can also create scarring under the skin and make surgery more difficult later, Dubrow cautioned — "so, ask whether a treatment is truly delaying a facelift or just delaying the decision."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
There is no "magic age" in terms of best results with a facelift, according to Dubrow.
"For some women, it is their late 40s. For others, it is their 50s or 60s," he said. "It comes down to genetics, skin quality and what is happening along the jawline and neck."
Advice for facelift timing can vary depending on what type of expert you see, and every specialist tends to see the problem through the treatments they perform, the doctor noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"A dermatologist may explain what can still be accomplished without surgery, and a board-certified plastic surgeon can tell you when those options have reached their limit … and when it is time to actually reposition the anatomy," he said.
Ultimately, he suggests getting opinions from both sides.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The right time should be based on your face, not the doctor’s menu," Dubrow said. "Choose what makes sense for your anatomy, your goals and your tolerance for surgery."
"The best facelift is the one nobody knows you had, but the best advice often comes from hearing more than one point of view."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Nearly 3 in 4 Americans are battling the same exhausting health problem, CDC reveals
summary: A neurologist explains how digital boundary erosion and constant scrolling are compounding mental fatigue and affecting sleep quality for Americans.
story: Fox News Senior Medical Analyst Dr. Marc Siegel emphasizes not obsessing about sleep, noting studies suggest 6-7 hours is typically ideal. He highlights deep sleep's vital function in brain detoxification, where microglia clean out metabolic waste and bad proteins. This restorative process reduces stress and improves heart health for many adults.
Exhaustion has become the default state for a vast majority of Americans.

Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Center for Health Statistics shows that more than seven in 10 U.S. adults experience fatigue over any given three-month period — a drain that public health officials say is taking a heavy toll on work and daily life.
The report, based on the 2024 National Health Interview Survey of roughly 27,000 adults, revealed that exhaustion is one of the most common health complaints nationwide.
COMMON BEDROOM MISTAKE COULD BE QUIETLY TAKING A TOLL ON YOUR HEALTH, EXPERTS SAY
The CDC defines fatigue as a state of physical or mental exhaustion that does not improve with rest, distinguishing it from simple sleepiness.
Overall, 71.5% of respondents reported feeling fatigued on at least some days, with 16.6% reporting "frequent fatigue" — defined as feeling exhausted most days or every day.
A report from the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics reveals that 71.5% of U.S. adults experienced fatigue over a three-month period, with 16.6% reporting frequent exhaustion. (iStock)
"Fatigue can be caused by numerous issues," Dr. Earnest Lee Murray, a board-certified neurologist at Jackson-Madison County General Hospital in Jackson, Tennessee, told Fox News Digital.

While underlying hormonal, cardiac or neurological conditions can play a role, "a vast majority of fatigue people experience is probably related to poor sleep quality as well as psychosocial stress, which a lot of times go hand-in-hand."
NIGHTTIME BATHROOM TRIPS COULD REVEAL HIDDEN HEALTH ISSUES — HERE'S WHEN TO WORRY
Frequent fatigue is significantly more common among women (20%) than men (13%).
The data also shows that younger adults ages 18 to 34 reported the highest rates of frequent exhaustion at 19.5%, while adults 65 and older reported the lowest rate at 12.9%.
Fatigue also increases among lower-income households, residents in rural areas and those living in the South and Midwest.
Experts say constant interruptions and digital multitasking can leave people feeling mentally drained. (iStock)

About 50.9% of adults with frequent fatigue reported having difficulties in three or more functional areas, including mood, mobility and memory. More than one-third of frequently fatigued adults said exhaustion limits their ability to work, while 29% reported cutting back on social activities.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Quality of sleep is very important for restoration of both the mental and physical body," Murray said. "The fatigue that results from poor quality of sleep contributes to slower thought processing, decreased concentration, and a less productive and happy workforce."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Although the report doesn't identify specific causes, experts say workplace culture and constant digital connectivity may contribute to fatigue.
"The advancements of instant communication technologies certainly have benefits; however, we are not able to disconnect from our work life any longer," Murray said.
Constant workplace connectivity, late-night communication and endless social media scrolling may undermine sleep quality by preventing the mind and body from fully disconnecting. (iStock)

"There are now expectation issues from work that can be dealt with quickly over our phone, even late at night. Also, social media and constant scrolling have certainly contributed to a reduced quality of sleep."

Experts say constant interruptions and digital multitasking can leave people feeling mentally drained. Research has found that frequently switching between emails, chat messages and other work tasks forces the brain to repeatedly refocus, contributing to mental fatigue.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"This report makes clear that fatigue is directly related to stressors and difficulty in life, and most importantly it interferes with function, work and socialization," Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel told Fox News Digital.
"This report makes clear that fatigue is directly related to stressors and difficulty in life."

"This data is analyzed independently of sleep or underlying medical problems," added the doctor, who was not involved in the study. "It emphasizes the importance of fatigue as an independent factor in predicting function and socialization."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
To combat the growing exhaustion, Murray stressed the need for setting boundaries and seeking medical evaluation as needed.

"It is important to disconnect from work and our electronic devices in the hours leading up to sleep," he advised. "Also, if fatigue is becoming a problem, it is important to seek medical attention to ensure there's no underlying medical reason contributing to the fatigue."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Champion athlete soils herself mid-race and keeps going, prompting fitness competition to change rules
summary: HYROX Beijing 2026 winner Joanna Wietrzyk faced online backlash after an incontinence incident during the race, prompting new competition rule changes.
story: 'Jesse Watters Primetime' visits the HYROX World Series of Fitness in New York, putting competitive athletes to the test.
A popular global fitness competition is changing its rules after an explosive incident at a Sept. 12 competition.
Australian professional athlete Joanna Wietrzyk won the race at HYROX Beijing — but the victory did not come without struggle.

During the race, Wietrzyk experienced fecal incontinence but continued competing. Despite the incident, judges and officials did not instruct her to stop, prompting concerns about potential health and safety risks for other competitors.
'A WIN IS A WIN' SAYS ATHLETE WHO DIDN'T LET A LITTLE DIARRHEA KEEP HER FROM FINISHING IN FIRST PLACE
The incident has sparked online debate — some people have supported Wietrzyk for her perseverance, while others suggested that her accident posed a potential biohazard.

The athlete first addressed the incident in a since-deleted Instagram post, reportedly writing in the caption, "Go hard or go home … a win is a win. In all seriousness, thank you for all the support. I’ll be back soon x."
Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes in HYROX Beijing 2026 at National Speed Skating Oval on Sept. 12, 2026, in Beijing, China. (VCG via Getty Images)
The athlete has since faced criticism from those who argue that her decision posed a health risk to other competitors.
In response, Wietrzyk released an official statement on Thursday, expressing her regret and announcing her retroactive withdrawal from the race.

"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing," she wrote in the statement posted on Instagram.

COULD 'HUMANMAXXING' ACTUALLY HELP YOU LIVE LONGER? HERE'S WHAT EXPERTS SAY"I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track … I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused."Wietrzyk continued, "I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away. On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned."
Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia takes part in HYROX Beijing 2026 at National Speed Skating Oval on Sept. 12, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Fred Lee/Getty Images)

Wietrzyk’s coach, Chris Bayens, previously posted a statement on social media in her defense. "What happened was an extraordinary set of circumstances that were unforeseen, rapidly evolving and almost impossible to fully comprehend in real time," he wrote on Instagram.
"Decisions were made under competition conditions by an athlete, judges and officials, all responding to a situation none of them could reasonably have prepared for."
Bayens continued that these decisions can be reviewed and lessons can be learned, but "judging someone’s intent, character or morality through the clarity of hindsight is neither fair nor honest."
FITNESS EXPERT VISITS GYMS NATIONWIDE, SHOUTS OUT 4 CLUBS FOR 'GETTING IT RIGHT'
"Sport occasionally produces moments that are imperfect and deeply human," he said. "Discussion is legitimate. The hatred and personal attacks that have followed are not."
Moritz Furste, co-founder of HYROX, also released a statement following the incident.

"I apologize to all that were directly or indirectly affected, as well as to everyone who felt like we did not handle the situation like we should have," he wrote. "HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end, it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not."
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS SIMPLE RULE TO GET IN SHAPE WITHOUT DREADING THE GYM: 'JUST MOVE'

The statement continued, "Of course, we started improving event processes, plus making rulebook changes immediately. As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again. We learn and try to get better every day."
What is HYROX?
According to HYROX, the race combines cardio with weight training, involving a total of eight kilometers (about five miles) of running and eight functional workout stations.

The structure of the competitions layers a one-kilometer run with one functional workout station, including SkiErg (a machine that simulates cross-country skiing), sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jumps, rowing, farmer's carry, sandbag lunges and wall balls.
Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia takes part in HYROX Beijing 2026 at the National Speed Skating Oval on Sept. 12, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Getty Images)

Launched in Germany in 2017, HYROX has grown rapidly worldwide, with recent reports putting participation at more than 1.4 million competitors globally. The organization describes the race as the world's fastest-growing fitness sport.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
More than 98% of HYROX competitors complete the race, with no time limit to finish and no qualification required to enter.
"The structure of HYROX eliminates the generic fear of ‘coming last,’" the brand wrote on its website.
Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia celebrates her victory in HYROX Beijing 2026 at National Speed Skating Oval on Sept. 12, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Fred Lee/Getty Images)
Physical risks
In an interview with Fox News Digital, California-based certified fitness trainer Ryan Read shared why the HYROX format can be so physically demanding.

"Your body doesn't get much time to fully recover between efforts," he said. "You may go from running directly to sled pushes, lunges or rowing. That forces your heart, lungs and muscles to work hard for a long period."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As the race progresses, maintaining proper form can become more difficult, according to Read, as the combination of intensity, duration and repetitive exercises can put a "significant amount of stress on the body."

"Muscles become fatigued, and the body uses up stored energy and fluids," he said. "During hard exercise, more blood is directed toward working muscles and away from the digestive system. That can make digestion more difficult."
"Real toughness also means knowing when your body is telling you to stop."
Running in particular creates a repetitive movement that can upset the stomach. Combining this with dehydration, heat and eating too close to competition can worsen symptoms, Read cautioned.
"This is why some athletes experience nausea, cramping, diarrhea or even vomiting during endurance events."
Participants compete in the burpee broad jumps event during the HYROX fitness race at the Bangkok International Trade and Exhibition Centre in Bangkok on March 21, 2026. (Amaury Paul/AFP)
There is a "big difference" between working through normal discomfort and ignoring a medical warning sign, according to the trainer.
Elite athletes are often conditioned to push through pain, a mindset that can intensify during competition. Adrenaline can also make it harder to recognize when the body is in distress, Read said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Symptoms like vomiting, fainting, severe chest pain or extreme weakness "should not be treated as proof that someone is working hard enough."
"Pushing through certain symptoms can turn a manageable problem into a medical emergency," he emphasized. "Real toughness also means knowing when your body is telling you to stop."

Read suggested that fitness organizations should have "clear rules" for when an athlete needs to be evaluated or removed from a competition, and medical staff should be easily accessible throughout the event.

"Equipment that becomes contaminated with vomit, blood or other bodily fluids should be taken out of use immediately," he said. "Simply wiping it quickly and sending the next competitor through may not be enough."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Bodily fluids can contain germs that may spread through contaminated surfaces or direct contact, Read said.
"The exact risk depends on the fluid, organism and type of exposure. Competitor safety should come before keeping the event moving on schedule."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Popular drugs for bone health linked to significantly lower Alzheimer's risk
summary: A Hong Kong study of 121,492 older adults links nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates for osteoporosis to a 16% lower Alzheimer's disease risk.
story: Dr. Janet Yoon, a pediatric oncologist and sarcoma specialist at City of Hope in Los Angeles, shares her thoughts on a cluster of rare cancer diagnoses in Ladera Ranch, Calif.
Commonly used osteoporosis drugs were linked to a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other types of dementia in a large study of older adults.

Among a group of 121,492 adults age 60 or older, the use of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBP) was associated with a 16% lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias compared to those who did not take osteoporosis medications.
The risk was 24% less compared to people taking other types of osteoporosis medications.
COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY

A nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate is a type of medication used to slow bone loss and reduce fracture risk, mainly in people with osteoporosis. Some common types include alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate and zoledronate.
Commonly used osteoporosis drugs were linked to a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other types of dementia in a large study of older adults. (iStock)

Osteoporosis occurs when the bones become weaker and more likely to break due to a loss of bone mass, according to the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS). The condition is especially common among older adults.

All adults in the Hong Kong study had recently been diagnosed with osteoporosis or suffered a serious fracture in the spine, humerus, wrist or hip. None had previously taken medication for osteoporosis.
3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS

"Emerging evidence points to a bone-brain axis, suggesting a close link between bone and brain health," study author Ching-Lung Cheung, associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong’s Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.

"Our previous studies and those of others have found that people with low bone mass or osteoporosis are more likely to develop dementia later in life. This highlights the importance of maintaining good bone health, which may also help reduce the risk of dementia."
Osteoporosis occurs when the bones become weaker and more likely to break due to a loss of bone mass. (iStock)
The study, which was published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia, was observational in design.
"Our findings therefore do not prove that bisphosphonate use reduces dementia risk; this needs confirmation in a clinical trial," Cheung said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Generalizability is another consideration, as our study involved only a Chinese population, and it remains uncertain whether the findings apply to other populations."
Another limitation is that baseline cognitive testing was unavailable, which means patients who already developed cognitive impairment may have been less likely to receive osteoporosis treatment.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The researchers also lacked information about the severity of participants’ osteoporosis and bone fractures and their use of over-the-counter calcium and vitamin D.
Other external factors, such as education level, social isolation, air pollution and vision loss, could also have affected dementia risk. (iStock)
Other external factors, such as education level, social isolation, air pollution and vision loss, could also have affected dementia risk, they acknowledged.

Although the study findings suggest that older patients receiving NBPs for osteoporosis or fragility fractures had lower rates of Alzheimer’s and related dementias, they do not yet justify prescribing bisphosphonates specifically to prevent or treat the disease.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The authors called for more research that will include wider populations with a focus on whether gender may play a role in the reduced risk.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The next step is to confirm our observational findings in a clinical trial," Cheung said. "If the benefit is demonstrated, it could have important implications for dementia management.
"We hope these findings encourage patients and healthcare professionals to weigh the overall benefits and risks and use appropriate treatment when indicated."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Rare cancer cases strike in California community as families demand answers
summary: At least six children in Ladera Ranch, California, have been diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma, prompting environmental testing and a state health review.
story: Dr. Janet Yoon, a pediatric oncologist and sarcoma specialist at City of Hope in Los Angeles, shares her thoughts on a cluster of rare cancer diagnoses in Ladera Ranch, California.
A cluster of rare cancer diagnoses has sparked concern and prompted environmental testing in Ladera Ranch, California, although state health officials say no specific cause has been identified.
At least six children in the area have been diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma, according to federal officials and local reporting.
This exceptionally rare cancer, which forms in the bone or nearby soft tissue, primarily occurs in adolescents and young adults, per the National Cancer Institute.
WOMAN LOSES BEST FRIEND TO OVARIAN CANCER, THEN RECEIVES SAME DEVASTATING DIAGNOSIS MONTHS LATER

"Knowing that this is a very rare cancer diagnosis amplifies the concerns," Dr. Janet Yoon, a pediatric oncologist and sarcoma specialist at City of Hope in Los Angeles, told Fox News Digital. "Anytime you hear of cases in a geographic location, it does raise some concerns ... I can completely understand why further investigation is being done."

A cluster of rare cancer diagnoses has sparked concern and prompted environmental testing in Ladera Ranch, California, although state health officials say no specific cause has been identified. (iStock)

Following the March 2026 death of 17-year-old Brody Matteson from complications of treatment for Ewing sarcoma, more families began speaking publicly about rare cancer diagnoses in the community, according to local reports.
Community seeks answers

Some residents – including Matteson's father, Dustin Matteson – have suggested the illnesses could be linked to the community's use of herbicides and pesticides, which prompted calls for a broader environmental investigation.
"We don't have a clear line of evidence for pesticides, but it is one of the things that concerns us," Matteson said to NBC Los Angeles in July.
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND

In 2024, prompted by residents’ concerns, the California Department of Public Health conducted a county-level review in an attempt to determine whether pesticide use in the community could have played a role in the development of certain cancer types.
"That analysis did not find an unusual pattern at the county level, but the data available at the time was​ limited," the CDPH stated on its website.
The agency is now conducting a second review of cancer incidence data for the Ladera Ranch area.

Following the March 2026 death of 17-year-old Brody Matteson from complications of treatment for Ewing sarcoma, more families began speaking publicly about rare cancer diagnoses in the community, according to local reports. (Matteson family)

"CDPH currently estimates the assessment will be completed in fall 2026, although the timeline may change based on the scope and complexity of the review and any additional information that may need to be evaluated," the agency stated.
"At this time, our colleagues at CalEPA (California Environmental Protection Agency) and its boards, departments and offices have not identified any immediate environmental hazards."
"We don't have a clear line of evidence for pesticides, but it is one of the things that concerns us."

The CDPH stated that it is not yet known whether diagnoses of Ewing sarcoma and other cancer types are higher than expected in the Ladera Ranch community – or whether environmental factors can increase the risk.

In July 2026, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli asked the Environmental Protection Agency to investigate possible environmental factors that could have contributed to multiple pediatric cancer cases.
According to federal officials and local reporting, at least six children in the area have been diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma. (iStock)

Over the summer, hundreds of residents gathered at community meetings. At the same time, Ladera Ranch Maintenance Corporation (LARMAC) – the master homeowners association (HOA) for the planned community of Ladera Ranch in Orange County – temporarily paused its use of certain landscape chemicals and formed an advisory committee to review its landscaping practices.

As the investigation has continued, some residents have also publicly reported diagnoses of other cancers, including glioblastoma, although the current state review has not established whether those cases are related.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
On Sept. 14, California State Fullerton researchers began collecting soil and water samples from local parks as part of the environmental investigation.

Jennifer Piazza, Ph.D., professor in the Department of Public Health at Cal State Fullerton, assembled a team of researchers to help address the environmental concerns stemming from the pediatric cancer cases.
Some residents have suggested the illnesses could be linked to the community's use of herbicides and pesticides, which prompted calls for a broader environmental investigation. (iStock)

"Environmental sampling is the first step of our larger, ongoing scientific investigation," she told Fox News Digital. "We are collecting soil and water samples across Ladera Ranch. They are being analyzed for heavy metals, such as arsenic and lead, as well as pesticides."
The team expects to have results by the end of the year, Piazza said.
"I also want to emphasize that whatever we find does not imply causality in terms of the pediatric cancer cases in Ladera Ranch," she added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
LARMAC released a statement to People magazine, extending its "heartfelt compassion to the families who have been affected by these devastating illnesses."

"LARMAC takes these concerns seriously. We are aware that public health agencies are reviewing available information, and we will continue to cooperate with those efforts and follow guidance provided by the appropriate health and regulatory authorities."
"It's pain that persists. It's pain that wakes them up from their sleep. It's pain that limits their daily activities."

"At this time, we are not aware of any determination by those agencies identifying a specific environmental cause or linking the Association’s landscape management practices to these illnesses," the statement read.
The organization also noted that it has reduced the use of synthetic pesticides and switched to organic pesticides.
What to know about Ewing sarcoma
"With Ewing sarcoma, there is no confirmed genetic or environmental cause that we know of," Yoon told Fox News Digital.
"We have not found any confirmed genetic or environmental factor that increases the likelihood of developing Ewing sarcoma."
Ewing sarcoma most often presents as persistent pain rather than a typical sports injury or growing pain, according to an oncologist. (iStock)

Some studies have linked occupational or high-level exposure to certain pesticides with an increased risk of several cancers, although the evidence varies by chemical and cancer type, according to the American Cancer Society.
No known lifestyle-related or environmental cause of Ewing sarcoma has been identified, the ACS states.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The disease most often presents as persistent pain rather than a typical sports injury or growing pain, according to Yoon.
"It's pain that persists. It's pain that wakes them up from their sleep. It's pain that limits their daily activities."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The doctor called cancer the "great masquerader" in children due to its rarity. "Growing pains are much more common than cancer," she added.

Yoon encouraged families to seek medical evaluation if pain is persistent, worsening or interfering with normal activities. Specialized cancer centers with sarcoma expertise can help ensure an accurate diagnosis, she advised.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Common antibiotic linked to higher risk of death in adults, major study finds
summary: A study of 110 clinical trials links the antibiotic cefepime to a 94.4% higher probability of all-cause mortality compared to other beta-lactam drugs.
story: A drug being developed to treat a serious lung disease may also help to slow the aging process, first author Alex Zhavoronkov, PhD, founder and co-CEO of Insilico Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
A commonly used drug has been linked to a higher risk of death in a new study.
The antibiotic, cefepime, which is used to treat bacterial infections like pneumonia, UTIs and skin infections, is typically administered via injection by healthcare providers in a clinical setting.

Severe side effects may include confusion, decreased consciousness or seizures, especially in older patients and those with kidney problems, among many other common symptoms, according to Mayo Clinic.
OLDER ADULTS TAKING 5 OR MORE PRESCRIPTION DRUGS FACE HIGHER RISK OF DEATH, STUDY FINDS
New research suggests the medication may be associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality.

The new global study, published in JAMA Network Open, reviewed 110 randomized clinical trials involving more than 22,000 patients who received cefepime or another beta-lactam antibiotic — a class of drugs that includes penicillins and cephalosporins.
Cefepime is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections like pneumonia, UTIs and skin infections. (iStock)

The patients included adults and children treated for febrile neutropenia — a medical emergency involving fever and dangerously low infection-fighting white blood cells — as well as pneumonia, severe bacterial infections, UTIs and meningitis.

Across all trials, 778 deaths occurred among 11,726 patients (6.6%) given cefepime, compared to 6.2% of patients given another antibiotic. Researchers evaluated deaths from any cause occurring within about 30 days of treatment.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS MEDICATIONS LINKED TO HIDDEN SIDE EFFECTS, STUDY FINDS
Using a Bayesian meta-analysis, the researchers found a 94.4% probability that cefepime was associated with higher all-cause mortality compared with other beta-lactam antibiotics.
When the analysis was limited to 73 peer-reviewed published trials, that probability increased to 98.6%.
The association appeared stronger in adults than in children, and was most pronounced among patients treated for febrile neutropenia.
Across all trials, 778 deaths of any cause occurred among 11,726 patients (6.6%) given cefepime, compared to 6.2% of patients given another antibiotic. (iStock)
Cefepime remains a commonly used broad-spectrum antibiotic for treating serious bacterial infections in hospitalized patients because it is effective against a wide range of bacteria.
The researchers did not recommend discontinuing cefepime, but called for additional guidance and research to better understand its safety.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The researchers said several factors could potentially explain the observed association between cefepime and higher mortality, although they were unable to identify a single cause.
Possible explanations include drug levels that are too low to effectively treat the infection and neurotoxicity, which can occur when drug levels become too high.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Researchers said finding the right dose of cefepime can be challenging, as higher doses may improve its ability to kill bacteria while also increasing the risk of toxic side effects.

The study had several limitations. It combined clinical trials that differed in design, patient populations, dosing strategies and comparison antibiotics, with some studies dating back decades. The analysis also found an association, not proof that cefepime itself caused the higher mortality.
Finding the right dose of cefepime can be challenging, as higher doses may improve the drug's ability to kill bacteria but also increase the risk of toxic side effects. (iStock)
Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, said the study demonstrates the importance of re-reviewing and analyzing older studies.

"In this case, it correctly pointed out that febrile neutropenia (low white blood cell count with a fever) is itself a big cause of death in this population, making it often difficult to determine if the treatment (cefepime) decreases or possibly increases this risk," Siegel, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A closer review of the data suggests that both underdosing and overdosing — rather than the drug itself — may be more closely linked to poorer outcomes and a higher risk of death, indicating that appropriate dosing may be the key, according to the doctor.
"I also think there may be a role for AI here in determining the exact right dose, as well as assessing outcome," Siegel suggested.

NYU doctor says, "Patients should not worry about cefepime, but they should continue to have discussions with their doctors and providers about the risks and benefits of the antibiotics that they need while they are sick." (iStock)
Isaac Dapkins, M.D., chief medical officer for the Family Health Centers at NYU Langone, noted that all medications carry risks and benefits, including antibiotics.

"Cefepime has an important role in the management of gram-negative bacterial infections," he told Fox News Digital. "Based on this article alone, patients should not worry about cefepime, but they should continue to have discussions with their doctors and providers about the risks and benefits of the antibiotics that they need while they are sick."

The doctor, who was also not involved in the study, noted that cefepime may be the only medicine available in certain cases, and patients who are sick enough to require the antibiotic have been "much better off" taking it compared to receiving no treatment at all.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"The article does not find a specific situation in which cefepime would not be the optimal option," he said. "Overall, we think this is a correlation, but not causation. There is a trend toward increased risk, but there is no clear understanding of which clinical situation."

"Therefore, if you, or your loved one, are sick enough to require IV antibiotics for a gram-negative infection, we would recommend following the doctor's recommendation for the antibiotic most likely to treat your illness."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Mysterious disease sending young, healthy Texas workers into kidney failure
summary: A mysterious chronic kidney disease devastating Central America's agricultural workers appears to have surfaced among Texas laborers in extreme heat.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'America's Newsroom' to discuss the rise in chronic kidney disease happening across the world, how to avoid it,and how weight loss drugs could benefit those who have it.
A mysterious form of kidney disease that has devastated young to middle-aged agricultural workers in Central America and South Asia appears to have surfaced in Texas.

Known as chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology (CKDu) — or Mesoamerican nephropathy — the condition continues to baffle researchers, as some otherwise healthy adults develop kidney failure without having any of the traditional risk factors.

Chronic kidney disease can range from mild to severe, potentially causing fluid buildup and increasing the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke and premature death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
CAN ALKALINE WATER ACTUALLY IMPROVE YOUR HEALTH? EXPERTS SEPARATE FACT FROM FICTION

But unlike typical cases, CKDu develops without common risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension and glomerulonephritis, a disease that inflames and damages the kidneys' filtering units, according to Dr. Gokul Paidi, a family medicine physician at Community Healthcare Network in New York.
"It typically strikes young to middle-aged adults, more often men, who work in agriculture and manual labor in hot, low-resource regions," he told Fox News Digital.
A mysterious form of kidney disease that has devastated young to middle-aged agricultural workers in Central America and South Asia appears to have surfaced in Texas. (Getty Images)
Several regional kidney diseases have been described over the decades, although not all are considered CKDu.

"Balkan endemic nephropathy has been documented since the 1950s, Itai itai disease in Japan was tied to cadmium contaminated rice, and Sri Lanka nephropathy has been studied since the 1990s," said Paidi, who has published a review on the condition.
Mesoamerican nephropathy – which was first described among sugarcane workers in El Salvador and Nicaragua in the late 1990s – is the form now being reported in the U.S., he noted.
"Disease often progresses rapidly over a few years, and dialysis and transplantation are rarely available."
Other locations have reported similar types of local epidemics, including Sri Lanka, India, rural Thailand and the Tierra Blanca area in Mexico, according to previous research.

"What’s emerging is that these are likely related conditions, essentially clusters of the same underlying disease process showing up in different farming and industrial regions around the world," Paidi said.
Unlike typical cases, CKDu develops without common risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension and glomerulonephritis, a disease that inflames and damages the kidneys' filtering units. (Getty Images)

Physicians at Houston safety-net hospitals, including Ben Taub, have treated otherwise healthy men in their 20s and 30s who presented with kidney failure — some with "Coca-Cola-colored urine," according to Texas Monthly.
They reportedly don’t have any of the typical risk factors that cause kidney disease, like high blood pressure or diabetes.
HEART ATTACKS AND STROKES RISING WITH EXTREME WEATHER EVENTS, RESEARCH SUGGESTS
"What’s striking about the Texas cases is how closely they mirror what we saw originally in Central America," Paidi noted.

The patients are largely undocumented laborers from Mexico and Central America working in construction, roofing and outdoor trades in extreme heat – jobs where water breaks are often limited, he added.

Physicians at Houston safety-net hospitals, including Ben Taub, have treated otherwise healthy men in their 20s and 30s who presented with kidney failure — some with "Coca-Cola-colored urine," according to Texas Monthly. (Getty Images)

According to a review of Harris County hospital records cited by Texas Monthly, roughly one in six emergency dialysis cases in uninsured or undocumented patients had no identifiable cause, "which is consistent with CKDu," Paidi told Fox News Digital.

Some patients are reluctant to seek care or participate in research because of their immigration status, making it harder to track the disease in Texas and detect kidney damage before it becomes irreversible, experts say.
Common symptoms of CKDu
Experts refer to CKDu as a "silent disease" because most patients don’t initially complain of any symptoms.

Most patients – especially those who work in sugarcane fields – learn they have the condition during routine screening blood tests, according to Dr. Richard J. Johnson, a leading expert on kidney diseases and emeritus professor of medicine at the University of Colorado.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Later, it can cause typical signs of severe chronic kidney disease, including fatigue, sleep disturbances, nausea, weakness [and] shortness of breath from anemia," he told Fox News Digital.
By the time symptoms appear, and the disease is diagnosed, many patients are approaching end-stage kidney disease. (iStock)
By the time symptoms appear, and the disease is diagnosed, many patients are approaching end-stage kidney disease.
Many affected people are located in resource-poor regions where dialysis and transplants are often unaffordable or inaccessible, which can increase the odds of premature death, Paidi noted.
Potential causes
Heat stress is considered one of the leading suspected drivers of the disease, although its exact cause remains unknown, according to Johnson.

Experts believe a combination of occupational and environmental factors may gradually damage the kidneys. Strenuous outdoor labor can lead to repeated heat stress and dehydration, potentially compounded by exposure to crop pesticides and smoke from burning sugarcane.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Workers may also contend with potentially unsafe drinking water and rely on over-the-counter NSAIDs for pain — factors that, combined with repeated dehydration and heat stress, could further strain the kidneys, according to Texas Monthly.
Some experts suggest that improving hydration and shade, reducing work hours and starting earlier in the day could reduce kidney damage.
Diagnosis and treatment
There is no specific test for CKDu. Doctors diagnose it by ruling out other causes of chronic kidney disease, along with a patient's occupational and environmental exposures, Paidi said.
"Kidney biopsy is the closest thing to a gold standard, but isn’t practical for widespread screening," he added.
Heat stress is considered one of the leading suspected drivers of the disease, although its exact cause remains unknown. (iStock)

There is no disease-specific treatment for CKDu. Management focuses on controlling blood pressure, avoiding additional kidney injury — including from NSAIDs — and using dialysis or kidney transplantation in advanced disease, according to Paidi.
Some patients receive ACE inhibitors — medications commonly used to treat high blood pressure — but these drugs can sometimes worsen kidney function in people who are dehydrated, Johnson cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Disease often progresses rapidly over a few years, and dialysis and transplantation are rarely available, so mortality is high," he added – which highlights the importance of screening for the condition.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
For people living or working in agricultural or outdoor labor jobs, especially in hot climates, Paidi recommends getting kidney function checked with a primary care doctor at least twice a year.
"A simple blood test for creatinine (a waste product normally filtered from the blood by the kidneys) and a urine test for protein can catch early changes long before symptoms appear," he advised.

title: Common bedroom mistake could be quietly taking a toll on your health, experts say
summary: A Tulane University study links sleeping with light on to higher risks of heart failure, atrial fibrillation, stroke and cardiovascular death.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," confirmed that household surroundings and ambient neighborhood conditions can directly interfere with restfulness.
A new study from Tulane University is raising fresh concerns about sleeping with a light on, linking nighttime light exposure to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

Researchers found that exposure to more than 3 lux of light — roughly the brightness of moonlight — was associated with increased risks of heart failure, atrial fibrillation (irregular and often very rapid heart rhythm), heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death.
Experts spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with sleeping with a nightlight.
THE DAYTIME HABIT THAT COULD TRANSFORM YOUR SLEEP, ACCORDING TO NEW STUDY

Sleep is partially controlled by the circadian rhythm, the brain’s internal 24-hour clock that regulates sleep and wakefulness, according to sleep expert and neuroscientist Chelsie Rohrscheib, Ph.D., a neuroscientist Neuroscientist and head sleep pesearcher at Wesper.
A new study from Tulane University is raising fresh concerns about sleeping with a light on, linking nighttime light exposure to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease. (iStock)

"The circadian rhythm is strongly influenced by light entering the eyes – light exposure signals the brain to suppress melatonin production, a hormone that helps regulate the timing of sleep, while low light levels signal the brain to produce more melatonin," the Michigan-based expert told Fox News Digital.
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID

"As melatonin levels rise in the evening, they help prepare the brain and body for sleep. Light pollution from various sources in our bedroom can trick the brain into producing less melatonin, which can negatively impact sleep quality."
Health concerns
Consistent light exposure will chronically reduce overall sleep quality, Rohrscheib warned.

"Sleep plays an essential role in many biological processes, including body and brain restoration, hormone release, immune system functioning, cognitive processes such as memory consolidation, brain waste clearance and metabolic regulation," she said.
FINDING THE SLEEP 'SWEET SPOT' COULD HELP YOU LIVE LONGER, STUDY SUGGESTS

"When sleep is consistently poor, these processes do not function optimally, which in turn elevates the risk for many chronic health conditions such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, obesity, neurodegenerative diseases, certain cancers and mood disorders."
Consistent light exposure will chronically reduce overall sleep quality, an expert warned. (iStock)

A 2022 Northwestern Medicine study found that just one night of sleeping with moderate light exposure (100 lux) disrupted glucose regulation while increasing heart rate and sympathetic nervous system activity, as reflected by reduced heart rate variability (HRV), Rohrscheib noted.
MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS
Sleep impairment is also linked to increased risk of mortality, according to Ashley Curtis, PhD, sleep researcher and assistant professor at the University of South Florida College of Nursing.

"Emerging evidence even suggests that it affects the gut microbiome, everything from digestion to immunity," she told Fox News Digital. "While the immediate evidence is strongest for disrupted sleep health, the downstream risks to your long-term health are substantial."
For people with insomnia, who already experience chronic sleep disruption, bright light exposure before bedtime can make these underlying problems worse. (iStock)
Certain groups may be more sensitive to nighttime light than others, experts agree.

"Shift workers, children, older adults and individuals with insomnia or mood disorders are especially vulnerable to the effects of light on sleep depth," Alex Dimitriu, M.D., a double board-certified sleep medicine doctor and founder of Menlo Park Psychiatry & Sleep Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Curtis noted that older adults often become less sensitive to light, meaning bright or short-wavelength light has a weaker effect on suppressing melatonin than it does in younger adults.
"The caveat, however, is that older adults also experience a higher baseline prevalence of sleep disruption, which can bidirectionally impact the circadian system," she added.
"While blackout curtains are recommended for optimal sleep, you don't need to have absolute darkness to maintain a healthy sleep environment," one expert said. (iStock)
There is also some evidence showing that bright light has a more pronounced impact on melatonin suppression in men, the expert noted.

For people with insomnia, who already experience chronic sleep disruption, bright light exposure before bedtime can make these underlying problems worse, as it further interferes with the biological circadian rhythm, Curtis warned.
What type of light is the worst?
Blue wavelength light from TVs and phones is the most disruptive because people’s retinas are most sensitive to it, and it maximally suppresses melatonin, according to Dimitriu.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Dim, warm, red-toned night lights cause far less circadian impact – these are natural sunset colors one would see in the evenings," he told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Curtis agreed that warmer, dimmer light, which has a longer wavelength, doesn't have as much impact on melatonin production.

"Research shows that even if dim light impacts melatonin initially, it allows time for the body to recover," she said. "Therefore, it doesn't disrupt your sleep to the degree that brighter light does."
Practical changes to improve sleep
"While blackout curtains are recommended for optimal sleep, you don't need to have absolute darkness to maintain a healthy sleep environment," Curtis said.
"Dim, warm, red-toned night lights cause far less circadian impact."
The experts recommend implementing the following changes to cultivate a healthy sleep environment – even if it’s not pitch black.
