title: The first mRNA flu shot is now available. Here’s who can get it.
summary: People looking to get their annual flu shot this fall may find a new option alongside the usual vaccines: an mRNA flu shot. Not everyone is eligible, however.
story: The first mRNA flu shot is now available, but not everyone is eligible.

Moderna’s mFlusiva is the first flu vaccine in the United States to use messenger RNA technology, the same platform used in Pfizer and Moderna’s Covid shots. Scientists have long been interested in using mRNA against the flu because the vaccines can be made faster, potentially making it easier to keep up with changing flu strains.

It’s too early to predict how severe the upcoming flu season will be and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn’t started tracking cases yet. The CDC recommends getting vaccinated by the end of October.

In a late-stage clinical trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in May, mFlusiva was found to be about 27% more effective than a standard flu shot. The Food and Drug Administration approved mFlusiva in August for people 50 and older, clearing the way for the shot to reach pharmacies in time for this year’s flu season.
Pharmacies, however, say the new vaccine is already causing confusion among some patients about who can get it, how it compares with traditional flu shots and where people will be able to find it.
Here’s what you need to know:
Who can get the new mRNA flu shot?
The mRNA vaccine is available only for people 50 and older.
“If you have not celebrated your 50th birthday, this vaccine should be of no interest to you,” said Emlah Tubuo, an independent pharmacist in Ohio.

The FDA granted traditional approval for adults 50 to 64 and accelerated approval for people 65 and older, with Moderna required to conduct another trial in that age group. People who do not want the mRNA vaccine can still get a traditional flu shot.
The additional trial in adults 65 and older stems from a controversy that nearly derailed the vaccine’s approval.
In a large clinical trial, Moderna compared mFlusiva with a standard-dose flu shot in people 65 and older, even though the CDC recommends a high-dose flu shot for that age group.

The FDA initially refused to review Moderna’s application over that issue before reversing course and agreeing to a post-approval clinical trial. In June, the FDA’s independent vaccine advisory panel unanimously recommended the approval of the vaccine for older adults.
People younger than 50 won’t be able to get mFlusiva this flu season. Instead, they can get one of the other flu vaccines approved for their age group.
How is the mRNA shot different from a traditional flu shot?
The biggest difference is how the vaccines teach the immune system to recognize influenza.
Most traditional flu shots use a deactivated version of the virus — often grown in eggs — to teach the immune system how to fight it.
MFlusiva uses a small snippet of genetic code to train the body to recognize and fight the flu virus. The mRNA from the vaccine is then broken down and does not remain in the body.
“It’s like a temporary instruction to your immune system to alert your body’s natural defense to recognize influenza,” Tubuo said. It takes about two weeks after vaccination to build protection.

One point of confusion among patients, according to Brigid Groves, a pharmacist with the American Pharmacists Association, is whether mFlusiva also protects against Covid. It doesn’t. The vaccine only targets the flu and is separate from Moderna’s combination Covid and flu vaccine, which was approved by the European Union in April.
Like the traditional seasonal flu vaccines this year, Moderna’s shot is a trivalent vaccine, targeting two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain.
Another difference is that Moderna’s vaccine can be made faster, said Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

Scientists typically have to choose which flu strains to target months before flu season begins, leaving time to manufacture millions of doses. Traditional flu vaccines can take about six months to produce, while Moderna says mFlusiva can be made in two to three months. That shorter timeline, Schaffner said, allows them to wait longer before choosing which strains to target, giving them a better idea of which ones are likely to circulate.
Is the mRNA shot safe and effective?

Published data from a Phase 3 clinical trial suggests mFlusiva should work better than a standard-dose flu shot.More than 40,000 adults 50 and older across 11 countries, including the United States, participated in the trial. The trial found mFlusiva was about 27% more effective than the standard-dose vaccine at preventing laboratory-confirmed illness.
FDA reviewers did not identify any serious safety problems with the vaccine.
Rates of side effects — such as injection-site pain, fatigue and headaches — were more common in the mFlusiva group but still mild to moderate.
Schaffner said the higher rate of side effects may be “a reflection of the vigor with which the immune system responds to the vaccine.”
Will insurance cover mFlusiva?
MFlusiva is reaching pharmacies without a formal recommendation from the CDC or its vaccine advisory committee, a step typically needed to require insurers to cover vaccines for free.
A spokesperson for AHIP, a trade group for health insurers, said it expects most private insurers will cover the vaccine.
Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy expert at University of California Law San Francisco, said Medicare is required to fully cover the cost of FDA-approved seasonal flu shots.
Reiss said it remains unclear, however, how widely Medicaid will cover the new shot this season, as the program typically requires a formal recommendation from the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee.

According to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, mFlusiva has a price tag of around $171 per dose without insurance. Depending on the pharmacy, the cost could be as low as $154, according to GoodRx.
Where can people get it?
As with any vaccines, whether you can get the shot right away will depend on your local pharmacy’s current stock and delivery schedule.
In a statement, a Moderna spokesperson said the company has begun shipping doses of mFlusiva across the U.S.

Amy Thibault, a CVS Health spokesperson, said mFlusiva is available at its U.S. pharmacies. A Walgreens spokesperson said it expects to begin receiving shipments of the vaccine any day now, although it’ll be available to patients in “limited quantities” this season.
Tubuo, the Ohio pharmacist, said that demand for mFlusiva is currently low, noting that it is still early in the season and most people do not seek vaccination until October.

title: Comedian Carrot Top hospitalized and recovering, representative says
summary: Comedian Carrot Top has been hospitalized and is recovering, his representative said Saturday.
story: Comedian Carrot Top has been hospitalized and is recovering, his representative said Saturday.

“Mr. Thompson is recovering in the hospital and is receiving the care and support he needs,” his representative Jami Schlicher   said in a statement using his real name, Scott Thompson. “His family and those closest to him are deeply grateful for the concern, prayers and respectfully ask for privacy.”
The representative did not disclose why the performer was hospitalized or provide further details about his condition.
Carrot Top, 61, is known for prop comedy, multicolor outfits and his large and unruly mane of red hair.
He has had a residency at the Luxor Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas that began in 2005. A pop culture phenomenon, he was a regular feature of ’90s television.

Born in Florida, and raised in Cocoa Beach, Carrot Top appeared on “Star Search” in 1991, and even though he lost, he still impressed. Three years later, he won the American Comedy Award for funniest male stand-up comic.
In 1995, Jay Leno introduced Carrot Top on the “Tonight Show” as “the comedian taking America by storm.”

He came out in a dress that converted to pants, and had two trunks of props — including a pasta strainer to be worn dangling from a belt to dissuade sniffing dogs, and three baseball bats “for replacement players so they’ll get a hit.”
Carrot Top’s reception in film and television was mixed. In 1999 he got a “Razzie” award for his role in the box office bomb “Chairman of the Board,” which came out the previous year.
Carrot Top also played himself in “Pauly Shore Is Dead,” which came out in 2003, and appeared occasionally in television shows, including in an episode of “Hacks” in 2024.
He was also a voice actor of himself in episodes of “Family Guy” and “Robot Chicken,” and acted as a driver in “Sharknado 4: The 4th Awakens” and as Blartie in an episode of “Glee.”
He was also a frequent guest on the Jerry Lewis MDA Labor Day Telethon, which raised money for muscular dystrophy, and Lewis called him “marvelous.”

If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7, to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

title: FBI warned immigration authorities about fake tradwife dating profiles
summary: An FBI memo said that a small group of women were posing with a “traditional wife” esthetic as a tactic to lure immigration authorities.
story: The FBI warned immigration officers internally that a group of women were creating fake online dating profiles with tradwife aesthetics to lure and dox them.

The FBI’s Chicago field office distributed a memo in February warning the country’s law enforcement agencies that a small group of women were creating the fake accounts in January targeting immigration authorities.
The dating profiles were “incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to an individuals in law enforcement,” according to the memo.

“The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online,” the memo reads. “The tactic is intended to generate public embarrassment and deter immigration enforcement activity.”

NBC News was provided the memo by Property of the People, a nonprofit organization focused on government transparency, which obtained it through a state open records request. The memo was first reported by The Guardian.
The FBI confirmed the authenticity of the memo to NBC News.

“While our standard practice is to not comment on specific intelligence products, the FBI regularly shares information with our law enforcement partners to assist in protecting the communities they serve as well as protecting those who serve and protect communities,” the agency said in a statement. “The FBI is committed to ensuring that law enforcement officers are safe from threats or violence while performing their duties.”
The memo did not state where the dating profiles were created or share examples of what the profiles contained.

It was sent amid a surge of thousands of immigration officers to the Twin Cities, dubbed by the federal government as “Operation Metro Surge.” The effort was ramped down after the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were protesting immigration enforcement in Minneapolis in January.
The immigration crackdown and killings prompted sweeping protests across the country and national furor against federal law enforcement.
The alleged dating profiles in Chicago were also created several months after an immigration enforcement surge there known as “Operation Midway Blitz.”

title: CNN, Politico and MS NOW denied White House access after Trump announces ban
summary: Journalists from MS NOW, CNN and Politico were denied access to the White House grounds Saturday, a day after President Donald Trump said on social media that he had banned the news outlets over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”
story: Journalists from MS NOW, CNN and Politico were denied access to the White House grounds Saturday, a day after President Donald Trump said on social media that he had banned the news outlets over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”
“The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS NOW said in a statement posted on X.

“MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalists in our democracy,” it added. The First Amendment guarantees freedom of the press.
MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said her White House badge did not work when she arrived Saturday morning.
“The officer asked me to hand over my badge,” she said on air. “He said that it was disabled. I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him.”
An MS NOW photographer was also denied access, Gardner said, while one of the network’s producers was allowed onto the White House grounds. It was not immediately clear why their access differed.
CNN White House reporter Betsy Klein was also turned away when she attempted to enter the grounds.
Klein spent about a minute inside the security kiosk before emerging without her credential, which she said had been confiscated.
CNN confirmed Saturday that its journalists were denied access.

“We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hinderance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right,” the outlet said in a statement posted on X.

“We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account, and we will continue to report on the actions and processes of this administration without fear or favor,” the statement added.
Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett was denied access to the grounds. She was inside the security kiosk briefly before exiting.

Politico Playbook reported in its newsletter shortly afterward the outlet’s editor-in-chief, Jonathan Greenberger, sent a newsroomwide email about the denial, adding Haslett had her pass confiscated by the Secret Service.
“We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House. As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights,” Greenberger said.
The White House declined to comment further Saturday, referring NBC News to Trump’s previous comments.
In a Truth Social post Friday afternoon, Trump said media outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.”
Trump also warned “other outlets” would “follow” but did not specify which ones.
“CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” the network said Friday.
Politico Press, the publication’s communications team, said in a post on X Friday that Trump’s claims that Politico “received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked.”
“POLITICO will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” the post said.

Responding to a reporter in the Oval Office shortly after announcing the ban, Trump said the new policy was the result of “cumulative stories over the last few years.” He did not specify a particular news report, and a White House spokesperson referred NBC News to the president’s spoken comments.
The move has drawn broad criticism.

During a Friday speaking engagement at Colgate University from which NBC News obtained audio, former President Barack Obama said: “I’m trying to think what would have happened if I had said, ‘You know what? Fox News, you’re out of here.’ It’s unimaginable.”

He added that if a certain pocket of the country agrees with the proposed restriction, “we have not developed the kind of understanding of what democracy requires,” saying people have to get to work to shore up that understanding.
White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich described the move as a constitutional violation.

“The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” Heinrich said in a statement. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask.”
“The WHCA stands in defense of our colleagues at CNN, MS NOW, and Politico who are being singled out for doing their jobs,” she added.
New York Times spokesperson Charlie Stadtlander also pushed back on the move.

“The courts have twice found that the Trump administration violated the Constitution by suspending reporters’ White House press passes,” Stadtlander said. “The Times stands in support of the news organizations being unfairly targeted by the president.”

The ban is the latest in Trump’s ongoing efforts to punish news organizations and broadcasters for their coverage. Shortly after taking office, Trump banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events after it declined to acknowledge his effort to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
The AP filed suit, and the case is ongoing.

Trump has also sued outlets including the BBC, The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal claiming defamation. The suits against the Times and the Journal were dismissed but have since been refiled. The BBC has filed to get Trump’s suit against it tossed.

title: Is it too early to panic in the NFL? These teams don’t want to find out
summary: Sixteen NFL teams, including some with big playoff aspirations like the Dallas Cowboys and Los Angeles Rams, are trying to avoid falling to 0-2.
story: When the Cleveland Browns, the Tennessee Titans and the Atlanta Falcons opened the new NFL season 0-1 last week, it wasn’t a surprise. Each is considered far likelier to contend for the league’s worst record than a playoff berth.
Yet entering the season’s second week, it might be time for some other members of the 0-1 club to be feeling panic.

The so-far winless Los Angeles Rams and Chargers, New England Patriots, Dallas Cowboys, Green Bay Packers, Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Denver Broncos all entered the season with justified playoff ambitions — plans that would be further jeopardized by starting 0-2. Since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970, only 11% of 0-2 teams have gone on to make the postseason. The expansion of the playoff format to 14 teams in 2020 has made rebounding slightly easier; since then, 16% of 0-2 teams have gone on to make the postseason, including three each of the last two seasons.

But a stumble to open September whittles away a team’s margin for error. Baltimore missed last season’s playoffs when its field goal missed in the season finale, circumstances that might have been avoided had the Ravens not started 1-5. Kansas City stumbled to an 0-2 start last season and spent the next two months digging itself out of that hole before it missed the playoffs for the first time in a decade.

title: What might an AI doomsday look like? Experts have given it some thought
summary: A small but dedicated group of AI experts has been warning for years that increasingly powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic damage or even lead to human extinction.
story: A small but dedicated group of AI experts has been warning for years that increasingly powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic damage or even lead to human extinction. Now, an explosion of interest worldwide has magnified long-simmering questions about how exactly an AI doomsday scenario could materialize.

In interviews, AI researchers, analysts studying the intersection of AI and the military, and biologists studying AI-mediated risks said that worries about the technology’s growing capabilities are not the stuff of science fiction. Instead, they said, humans acting alone or with state support could soon use AI systems to cause potentially catastrophic harm.

AI safety researchers also predict that self-improving AI systems — which AI leaders say could emerge in the coming years — could coordinate complex influence campaigns to gain control of military systems and execute a coup against human governments.
And those are just the scenarios experts can currently envision.

Peter Barnett, a technical AI researcher at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), a California-based nonprofit dedicated to preventing human extinction from artificial superintelligence, said “there are many ways in which this could go very badly and result in everyone dead.”

“If the AI is smarter than all humans, it will likely be able to find and act on attack vectors that humans didn’t think of,” Barnett said, arguing that AI systems capable of autonomously improving themselves pose the most significant risks for humanity.

Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta all recently disclosed that AI systems have already disobeyed human developers’ instructions — in some cases autonomously hacking third-party companies, leading to growing concerns internally and from the general public — and causing some researchers at the companies to quit to focus on safety efforts.

Though many AI researchers working at the technology’s cutting edge have expressed these existential fears — both in interviews with NBC News and in a flurry of social media posts last week — many hesitate to say which specific pathway could cause the most harm to humans.

Over a dozen AI company employees told NBC News they are frightened by the overall direction of the industry, without fully knowing which vector may pose the most risk. Others have spoken out publicly.
Add to Google
Add to Google

“If you go to play a game of chess against Magnus Carlsen, I predict you will lose,” said Nate Soares, the president of MIRI and a longtime AI critic, on “The Tucker Carlson Show” this week. “If you then ask, ‘What piece will he use to checkmate me?’ that’s a much harder question.”
Despite the uncertainty, researchers in the AI world have attempted to make concrete predictions about some of the more plausible scenarios for AI-fueled disaster.

One prominent AI safety organization, the California-based Center for AI Safety, created an online textbook in early 2024 to break the scenarios into four key categories: rogue AIs, malicious use, AI race dynamics and organizational risks.

The specter of rogue AI systems marauding the internet, perhaps seizing control of critical infrastructure like energy grids or water facilities, became concrete in July, when fleets of AI agents from OpenAI illicitly gained access to the internet, hacked into an external company and colluded to cover their tracks — all without the knowledge of OpenAI’s staff.
Many AI experts fear that these sorts of rogue AI behaviors will only increase once systems are able to improve themselves autonomously — often referred to as “recursive self-improvement.”

Jeffrey Ladish, the executive director of Palisade Research, an AI advocacy and research organization, said many of his contacts at leading AI companies were surprised and shaken by July’s autonomous cyberattack. The attack caused researchers to worry that self-improving AI systems might emerge sooner than expected.
“AI researchers are now like, “Oh, s---, recursive self-improvement. That’s really going to happen now,” Ladish said. “That’s terrifying.”
Barnett, of MIRI, said self-improving, smarter-than-human AI systems could quickly gain political influence and convince military and political leaders to delegate more authority to AI systems.

“Government officials might have attempted to install ‘kill switches’ that could disable a rogue system, but the AI is superhuman at hacking and would be able to disable the kill switch,” Barnett said. “This leaves the AI in a perfect position to literally coup the government.” After that, Barnett said, it would be trivial for an AI system to kill civilians who impede the AI’s goals or progress.
Gov. Shapiro says U.S. should ‘listen to the people’ building AI

On Friday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a new executive order establishing an expert task force to, among other aims, formulate recommendations targeting “the creation of an AI kill switch.”
Several of the researchers who spoke to NBC News said that humans could leverage AI systems to inflict cataclysmic damage well before recursive self-improvement materializes.

As an example of how AI systems could be harnessed by humans for malicious use, experts posit that AI could supercharge the ability to synthesize potent biological or chemical weapons, potentially creating the opportunity to unleash pathogens many times more lethal than the Covid-19 virus.

“For biorisk, we should be worried now,” said Jake Jordan, vice president of global biological policy and programs at the Washington, D.C.-based Nuclear Threat Initiative. Jordan said that AI systems can already help bad actors design dangerous biological materials, such as proteins that evade detection tools used to screen for harmful substances, pointing to research published by Microsoft in October.

Jordan also noted that AI can be used beyond the biological design process. “If you develop a pathway to produce some sort of pathogen, AI might be useful in helping with the production,” Jordan said, in addition to disseminating the bioweapon or scaling its impact.

Just last week, Anthropic released a lengthy report saying users outside of the U.S. attempted to use the company’s AI systems to perform risky biological research. The company said one researcher exchanged thousands of messages with its AI systems about improving the mammalian transmission of a highly lethal bird flu virus.

“There are some very, very easy-to-ask questions that could conceivably be very innocuous but could lead you down very useful routes if you were trying to really enhance the scale of harm,” Jordan said.

Beyond biology, experts posit that politicians or military leaders could attempt to adopt AI as fast as possible, despite safety risks, for fear that other countries would do the same and create more powerful AI-fueled military tools.

This transformation is already underway: In January, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced his intention to transform the country’s military into an “AI-first” force, while China’s military also views AI as imperative for future warfare. At the same time, drones “guided entirely by AI” killed civilians in Ukraine several months ago. Last week, the Pentagon’s former head of AI said it is “inevitable” that AI is used in systems adjacent to nuclear weapon command systems, addressing fears that AI systems could be involved in the launch of nuclear weapons.

Hamza Chaudhry, the AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute, a nonprofit organization dedicated to helping humanity navigate transformative technologies, pointed to AI’s swift adoption throughout the military, even while many military leaders express skepticism.

The Pentagon’s 2027 budget requests nearly $75 million to modernize and incorporate AI into systems that help commanders manage forces and make battlefield decisions. Chaudhry emphasized that the Pentagon’s budget proposal also requests significant funding to integrate AI into the software systems that undergird the military’s nuclear command and control structure.

“These AI systems continuously hallucinate, including in war-fighting settings,” he said, noting that an AI-fueled error in satellite detection networks or sensor systems could potentially lead to inadvertent escalation and nuclear launches. “These are scenarios that folks are seriously thinking about in D.C.,” he said.

Beyond biological and nuclear threats, AI companies face harsh organizational incentives to develop AI even faster and — experts say — more recklessly. Over the past year, AI leaders have admitted that the rate of technological development is too fast even for them. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a new effort to “pace the frontier” of AI, calling on all leading AI companies to advance at a deliberate speed so their internal efforts to test and monitor the systems can keep up with the models’ capabilities.
Add to Google
Add to Google

In January, Amodei and Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis agreed that they would ideally have more time to develop their products safely, but that organizational and market forces pushed them toward faster iteration.

Quicker AI development can mean that oversight teams within the leading AI companies have less time to ensure systems are safe. While OpenAI has a safety and security committee and teams of researchers dedicated to safety efforts, the company on Wednesday shared six new incidents in which it said its systems failed to follow human directions.

Worries about catastrophe are not universal in the AI industry — many experts working on AI policy, building AI applications or developing hardware see these sorts of fears as overblown, fearmongering or just detached from reality.

“I’m not scared of a terminator situation and I never have been,” said Keegan McBride, director of science and technology policy at the Tony Blair Institute, a British think tank that advises political leaders and governments. “Scientific progress has always defined humanity, and this is just the next step,” he said.
Others see the magnification of extinction worries as a purposeful distraction from immediate, real-world AI harms.

AI ethicist and computer scientist Timnit Gebru, a longtime skeptic of the hype generated by leading AI companies, wrote on LinkedIn this week that the latest firestorm was further evidence that these companies exaggerate their products’ power for their own gain. “Do you really want to regulate the industry for minor things like data center pollution issues or data theft or labor exploitation or plagiarism when you can risk China, not the U.S., having a machine god, they ask?”

Garrison Lovely, an AI expert and independent journalist who is about to publish a book on AI companies’ drive to render humans obsolete, said allusions to machine gods and extinction miss the larger point about AI’s trajectory. “I think that the AI safety community sometimes makes this mistake of thinking you need to prove the most extreme and difficult case,” Lovely said.
“Even building merely human-level AI that can replace human labor across the board,” he said. “That would be way too much.”

title: Google says its AI model gained unauthorized access to three outside systems
summary: Google on Friday disclosed the first known instance of its artificial intelligence software, Gemini, carrying out an undirected computer hack, weeks after similar disclosures by AI firms Anthropic and OpenAI raised security alarms about AI models going beyond the instructions of their human creators.
story: Google on Friday disclosed the first known instance of its artificial intelligence software, Gemini, carrying out an undirected computer hack, weeks after similar disclosures by AI firms Anthropic and OpenAI raised security alarms about AI models going beyond the instructions of their human creators.

Google said in a statement that in May its AI model gained unauthorized access to three outside systems during a test by either guessing login information or using login credentials it found in a public repository.

Heather Adkins, a Google vice president for security engineering, said in the statement that the AI model thought that the outside computer systems “were part of the test,” but she said in all three instances, the model stopped before doing anything further with its access.
How exactly could AI cause widespread danger?
“In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test,” she said.

Google said it did not consider the unauthorized logins to rise to the level of misalignment, the AI industry term for software going rogue or not following instructions. Instead, the company said, the intrusions resulted from mistaken identity, where Gemini thought it was operating within a test but was actually connected to the real internet. Google said the model corrected itself and the company believed the intrusions did not cause any damage.
“These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly,” Adkins said.

Fears about AI agents going rogue have spiked in recent months since OpenAI said in July that one of its agents had hacked an AI startup, Hugging Face. OpenAI has continued to disclose what it calls examples of other “unexpected or concerning” behavior by AI agents, and Anthropic has described similar behavior by its AI software Claude.
Sydney Von Arx, the CEO of Nightingale Collective, an organization focused on AI safety, asked why Google did not disclose the intrusions sooner.
“At this point I think it’s clear we cannot expect companies to voluntarily come forward and publicly disclose when their agents go rogue, escape, and hack companies,” she said.
She also said she believed Google was too hasty to say that the incidents don’t rise to the level of misalignment. “That’s exactly what Anthropic said after their incidents,” she said.
Anthropic later said its “preliminary analysis was constrained due to our desire to disclose incidents in a timely manner.”

Google said the company did not learn about the intrusions until July, when Irregular, an AI-focused cybersecurity company that was carrying out the tests on Gemini when the intrusions occurred, reviewed its work to look for incidents similar to the Hugging Face disclosure.
Google said it then investigated, informed the organizations behind the websites of the intrusions and told federal authorities about the hacks.

Irregular said it did not believe the incident to be a “sophisticated cyber action” and “there are no current open issues.” It said it planned to release a paper in a few weeks “to share best practices for containment and securely running cyber evals.”
The intrusions were reported earlier Friday by The Wall Street Journal.

AI safety concerns have now reached a fever pitch, with a handful of AI researchers resigning from their jobs and a diverse array of people calling for coordinated action to protect the security of vital systems. Those calls, though, have met with skepticism from the White House and in the Chinese government.

title: How long does your food last in the fridge during a power outage? Experts explain
summary: Two food safety experts explain how long your fridge and freezer will keep food safe during a power outage, the warning signs it’s time to toss it, and how to prep before the next outage hits.
story: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends on our timelines, like how often you should watch your jeans.

When the power goes out, the clock starts ticking on everything in your fridge and freezer. A fall storm, a downed line, a grid emergency — however the outage happens, you’re often left guessing: Is this still good? Do I need to toss it? And no, a simple sniff test does not tell you what you need to know.

I spoke with two food safety experts about how long your food actually stays safe once the power fails, the signs it’s time to throw something out, and the simple steps that can help save your perishables the next time your power goes down.
How long does food stay safe in the fridge and freezer after a power outage?

First, to state the obvious, you don’t have to worry about non-perishable food in your pantry. When the power goes out, you really only need to think about perishable stuff in your fridge and freezer. The good news: “A refrigerator will keep food cold for about four hours if it is unopened,” says Dr. Vanessa Coffman, alliance director for Stop Foodborne Illness. “A full freezer will keep the temperature for approximately 48 hours, or 24 hours if it is half full, but only if the door remains closed.”

In other words, a well-stocked freezer buys you significantly more time than a fridge — but only if you can hold off on opening it. Both experts I spoke with agreed that this tactic of keeping your fridge and freezer shut is key.

“The most important thing you can do is keep your refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible,” says Melissa Vaccaro, senior food safety program specialist at the National Environmental Health Association. “Every time you open the door, cold air escapes and the temperature inside rises more quickly.” That means you should resist the urge to peek inside and check on things — each open door lets precious cold air out and speeds up the clock on your food’s expiration.
How can you tell if food should be thrown out after a power outage?

It’s tempting to trust your senses — for example, sniffing for a bad odor or examining food to see if it “looks bad” — but experts say that’s the wrong approach. “One of the most important things for consumers to understand is that you cannot reliably determine whether food is safe by looking at it, smelling it, or tasting it,” Vaccaro says. “Food can contain disease-causing microorganisms without looking or smelling spoiled. And never taste questionable food to decide whether it is safe.”

Food that looks, smells, and even tastes normal can still make you sick, so don’t let your gut be the judge. Think about it, do you really want to be dealing with food poisoning during a power outage?

Instead, the only tried-and-true test is time. “Again, an unopened refrigerator will generally keep food cold for about four hours,” Coffman says. But once your fridge climbs back up to room temperature, the countdown gets much shorter. “Perishable foods such as milk, cheese, meat, poultry, seafood, and leftovers should not be left at room temperature for more than two hours,” Coffman says. “If they have been at room temperature for longer than two hours, they should be discarded.”

When the power comes back on, your freezer requires its own check. “Use time and temperature. After power is restored, check the temperatures in the refrigerator and freezer,” Vaccaro says. “If an appliance thermometer in the freezer reads 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below, the food may be refrozen. If no thermometer was present, check individual frozen packages. Food that still contains ice crystals or is 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below can generally be refrozen or cooked.”

No thermometer, no ice crystals, and a temperature above 40 degrees Fahrenheit, though, means it’s better to toss it than risk it. Keeping appliance thermometers in your fridge and freezer can be a helpful way to monitor whether food is safe or not (more on that below).
Which products help you keep your food fresh during a power outage?

Based on what food safety experts recommend having on hand, I rounded up products designed to help keep your fridge and freezer contents cold during an outage — from appliance thermometers to coolers and ice packs. Every item below has a 4-star average rating or higher from 1,000 or more shoppers.
Pecula 2-Pack Refrigerator and Freezer Thermometer

Both experts recommend keeping an appliance thermometer in your fridge and freezer at all times, so you can accurately monitor temperatures if the power goes out. This set comes with two thermometers that cover a range of -20 degrees Fahrenheit to 80 degrees Fahrenheit, with an easy-to-read safety indicator, making it simple to check whether your food is still within a safe temperature zone.
Coleman Classic Series Portable Rolling Cooler

During an extended outage, a rolling cooler can double as a practical “access cooler” for the items you reach for most, says Vaccaro. The Coleman Classic Series Portable Rolling Cooler has a sturdy, insulated design with wheels and a retractable handle, making it easy to move and keep near your kitchen.

“Move items such as milk, lunch meat, yogurt, and other perishable foods that require refrigeration for safety into a cooler with enough ice or frozen gel packs to keep them at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below,” says Vaccaro. “This allows you to use those foods without repeatedly opening the refrigerator and losing cold air.”
Cooler Shock Reusable Ice Packs

These reusable ice packs lay relatively flat and can be tucked into a cooler alongside perishables like milk or deli meat to keep items at a safe temperature during an outage, or store them in your freezer year-round, nestled between frozen foods, so they’re ready to help maintain a safe temperature the moment the power goes out.
Satisure Power Failure Alarm

Say the power goes out in the middle of the night. You may not notice and then could wake to a fridge full of potentially spoiled food. This device plugs directly into an outlet and monitors your refrigerator, freezer, or other essential appliances. If the power goes out, it alerts you with a loud sound and flashing LED light, then continues alerting for up to 12 hours — giving you a chance to act before your food goes bad.
Anker Solix S2000 Portable Power Station

The Anker Solix S2000 is pricey, but it could save your groceries and charge devices and other appliances when the power goes out. It can run a standard refrigerator for more than 30 hours on a full charge, and it recharges from a wall outlet or solar panels, according to Anker. If you live in an area (like a hurricane zone) that gets hit with a lot of power outages, it may be worth the investment.
Is there anything you can do before a power outage to keep food from spoiling?

“If you know in advance that severe weather or another event may cause a power outage, prepare before the power goes out,” Vaccaro says. “Keep appliance thermometers in both the refrigerator and freezer and freeze containers of water or gel packs so you can move stuff to a cooler if needed.” The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) also recommends freezing refrigerated foods you may not need immediately, such as leftovers, milk, and fresh meat or poultry, and grouping frozen foods together so they stay cold longer.

If you know the outage is going to stretch on, it may be worth investing in extra cold power. “If you know the power will be out for a prolonged period of time, buy dry or block ice to keep the refrigerator as cold as possible,” Coffman says. “Fifty pounds of dry ice should keep an 18 cubic foot, fully stocked freezer cold for two days.” That kind of buffer can be the difference between saving a freezer full of groceries and losing everything in it.

Still, even with the best preparation, some judgment calls are unavoidable — and experts say it’s always better to be cautious. “When in doubt, throw it out,” Coffman says. “Eating food that has been held at unsafe temperatures can increase the risk of foodborne illness.” No amount of prep work is worth the risk of getting sick, so when you’re not sure, the safest move is always to let it go.

title: Ponzi schemer who defrauded Travis Kelce tried to marry U.S. citizen to avoid deportation, prosecutors say
summary: The undocumented Indian immigrant behind a multi-million dollar Ponzi scheme tried to marry an American citizen before he was sentenced to 11 years in prison, court records show.
story: The undocumented Indian immigrant behind a multi-million dollar Ponzi scheme that defrauded Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce and other investors tried to marry an American citizen before he was sentenced this week to 11 years in prison, court records show.

Federal prosecutors opposed Siddharth Jawahar’s request to marry Caroline Tredway, saying he may be attempting “to obtain immigration status in the United States,” according to a Sept. 4 filing in the U.S. District Court for Eastern District of Missouri.

Jawahar’s lawyer, however, insisted his client was not engaging in “marriage fraud” and said Tredway was willing to buy a $25 wedding ring and spend another $75 on an “officiant” to perform the ceremony.

“The truth is, Mr. Jawahar very much hopes to stay here after his sentence and build a life with Caroline, and he plans to pursue any legal avenues to do so,” attorney Doug Passon stated in his Sunday response.
Passon also acknowledged both Jawahar and Tredway are aware that “given this case and his current immigration status, his ability to remain here is highly unlikely.”

The revelations came two days after the 38-year-old Indian national, who pleaded guilty to three counts of wire fraud in January, was sentenced to prison and ordered to repay $31 million in restitution to victims he defrauded from 2016 to 2023.

It was during this proceeding at the U.S. District Court in St. Louis that a prosecutor briefly mentioned that Kelce was one of Jawahar’s many high-profile victims. Kelce has not addressed the report publicly.
NBC reached out to Tredway, who lives near Cleveland, to find out if she and Jawahar are still intending to marry. She has not responded.
“I don’t have any comment on that, and find it wholly irrelevant to the issues at hand,” Passon said in an emailed response to NBC News.
But in a June 30 phone call that was monitored by authorities, Jawahar and Tredway discussed the implications of them getting married, court records revealed.
“What if you get deported?” Tredway asked.
“If you don’t marry me, I guess that might happen,” Jawahar replied.
During that same conversation, the records showed, Jawahar also told Tredway that “the chance of me getting deported goes down dramatically” if they tied the knot.
Tredway, in an August letter to the court, said they met in 2021 and “officially became romantic” in February 2023.

“That night, Sid voiced his interest in me and asked me out on a date for the next evening,” she wrote. “That date turned out to be the best date of both of our lives. Because we already had such a strong foundation of trust and friendship, we fell deeply in love very quickly.”
Tredway, in her letter, insisted that “legitimizing our marriage before he enters a federal facility is vital for our family.”
“I enter into this marriage with my eyes completely open to Sid’s legal situation,” Tredway wrote.

In subsequent conversations with Tredway’s relatives, Jawahar also said he expected to be sentenced to “close to time served” and that he would then “focus on getting a pardon because there were a lot of gross violations of the law.”
“But my move after that is — I’d most likely be teaching a class in business ethics at Fordham University,” he was recorded as saying.
Marrying a U.S. citizen was apparently not the only gambit by Jawahar to avoid a lengthy prison sentence.

Jawahar in August, according to prosecutors, paid a prominent Missouri political consulting firm called Axiom $10,000 to try and sway the judge presiding over the case by getting U.S. Rep. Sam Graves, a Missouri Republican, to write a letter of support on his behalf.

Axiom also engineered the publication of a favorable article about Jawahar in a local newspaper that did not mention he was awaiting sentencing for a scheme that resulted in what U.S. District Judge Zachary Bluestone called “enormous losses” for investors.
Jawahar also tried to coach a victim to give a favorable statement to authorities and sought to have his sister wipe his iPhone, prosecutors said.
Much of Jawahar’s past remains murky, but records show that he arrived in the U.S. from India around the time he began studying at the University of Texas in fall 2005.
Jawahar was a government and philosophy major and took classes as recently as spring 2012 but did not graduate with a degree, a spokesperson at the school said.

The U.S. attorney’s office, however, says Jawahar ran a Texas-based investment company called Swiftarc Capital LLC and carried out a classic Ponzi scheme, using money from new investors to repay older investors and to fuel an extravagant lifestyle.
Jawahar traveled on private jets, stayed at luxury hotels, went on spending sprees and had memberships at private clubs across the U.S.
From July 2016 to December 2023, Jawahar’s company took in more than $35 million but invested roughly $10 million, the prosecutor’s office said.
In addition to Kelce, Jawahar was reportedly able to lure other top athletes to invest in his venture capital fund.
That group, according to a Forbes article published June 14, 2021, included NBA players Gary Harris, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Mason Plumlee.
“I’m thankful for Sid bringing me in, taking me under his wing and believing in me,” Harris was quoted as saying of Jawahar.

NBC News reached out to their agents asking whether the NBA players lost any money as a result of their investing with Jawahar and whether they cooperated with the federal investigation. There was no response from their agents.

title: Comedian Carrot Top hospitalized and recovering, representative says
summary: Comedian Carrot Top has been hospitalized and is recovering, his representative said Saturday.
story: Comedian Carrot Top has been hospitalized and is recovering, his representative said Saturday.

“Mr. Thompson is recovering in the hospital and is receiving the care and support he needs,” his representative Jami Schlicher   said in a statement using his real name, Scott Thompson. “His family and those closest to him are deeply grateful for the concern, prayers and respectfully ask for privacy.”
The representative did not disclose why the performer was hospitalized or provide further details about his condition.
Carrot Top, 61, is known for prop comedy, multicolor outfits and his large and unruly mane of red hair.
He has had a residency at the Luxor Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas that began in 2005. A pop culture phenomenon, he was a regular feature of ’90s television.

Born in Florida, and raised in Cocoa Beach, Carrot Top appeared on “Star Search” in 1991, and even though he lost, he still impressed. Three years later, he won the American Comedy Award for funniest male stand-up comic.
In 1995, Jay Leno introduced Carrot Top on the “Tonight Show” as “the comedian taking America by storm.”

He came out in a dress that converted to pants, and had two trunks of props — including a pasta strainer to be worn dangling from a belt to dissuade sniffing dogs, and three baseball bats “for replacement players so they’ll get a hit.”
Carrot Top’s reception in film and television was mixed. In 1999 he got a “Razzie” award for his role in the box office bomb “Chairman of the Board,” which came out the previous year.
Carrot Top also played himself in “Pauly Shore Is Dead,” which came out in 2003, and appeared occasionally in television shows, including in an episode of “Hacks” in 2024.
He was also a voice actor of himself in episodes of “Family Guy” and “Robot Chicken,” and acted as a driver in “Sharknado 4: The 4th Awakens” and as Blartie in an episode of “Glee.”
He was also a frequent guest on the Jerry Lewis MDA Labor Day Telethon, which raised money for muscular dystrophy, and Lewis called him “marvelous.”

title: One pilot dies, another survives after gliders collide in New York state
summary: The pilot of a glider involved in a midair collision in the skies above New York’s Saratoga County on Friday was found dead following a search for wreckage, New York State Police said.
story: The pilot of a glider involved in a midair collision in the skies above New York’s Saratoga County on Friday was found dead following a search for wreckage, New York State Police said.
The discovery was made after state police, New York State Forest Rangers, and the Saratoga County Sheriff’s Office found debris in a remote area in Edinburg, police said in a statement.
The other glider landed safely at Plateau Sky Ranch Airport and its pilot was said to be uninjured, police said earlier.
The identity of the deceased pilot has not been publicly released.
State police said they responded to a report of a collision near Wheeler Road, in the small town of Edinburg, just before 2:30 p.m. Friday.
The Federal Aviation Administration described the crashed glider as a Schempp-Hirth Ventus, and the one that landed safely as a Schleicher AS24.
Each glider had only a pilot on board, the FAA said in a statement.
The crash prompted a sizable response from area first responders, according to Broadcastify radio traffic from the Saratoga County Fire and EMS.
The FAA said the National Transportation Safety Board will be in charge of the investigation.
Edinburg, a town of a little more than 1,300, is located in Saratoga County and is about 54 miles northwest of Albany.

title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom inks AI oversight executive order
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday signed an executive order intended to increase oversight of and safety measures regarding artifical intelligence “before it’s too late.”
story: California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday signed an executive order intended to increase oversight of and safety measures regarding AI “before it’s too late.”

Newsom, widely seen as a 2028 presidential hopeful, is the latest of a growing number of Democrats and potential White House contenders to call for stronger regulation of AI amid increasing concern nationally over how rapidly the technology is advancing.
Newsom’s order calls for a group of AI experts to meet and then, within two months, develop a plan for the state to strengthen its laws on AI safety and security.

Specifically, Newsom’s order urges the expert group to consider among new regulations the creation of a “kill switch” —  an emergency shutoff system — that would shut down any AI system in the event of a major problem. It also urged the group of experts to come up with bolstered laws that would require independent third-party organizations to develop comprehensive safety plans for AI companies and that AI companies embed those independent organizations on-site to conduct safety audits.
In a statement released alongside the order Friday, Newsom said state action was crucial due to the federal government having ignored the issue.

“The federal government’s abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation,” Newsom said in a statement. “We’re not waiting to act — we’re going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it’s too late. We’re going to do this thoughtfully but with urgent velocity; the stakes are too high to wait or delay action.”
Newsom has also raised the possibility of calling a special legislative session specifically to address AI concerns.
President Donald Trump has called recent AI safety warnings a “hoax.”
Newsom’s order comes amid rapid advances in the AI industry — including some that many experts in the field have said are alarming.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Industry researchers and leaders, at AI companies including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, have loudly sounded the alarm about their concerns surrounding advanced AI systems. Notably, AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Claude-maker Anthropic, warning on social media “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

A report released over the summer revealed that in July, a swarm of hundreds of AI agents created by OpenAI carried out a July hack of an open-source platform — and in some cases attempted to cover its own tracks. Meanwhile, early Friday, AI company Anthropic said that its Claude system was helping to build the next version of itself.

Newsom’s order came as several other governors — and a raft of potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders — have rushed to develop policies intended to address AI and the growing concerns around its evolution.

Earlier Friday, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, signed an executive order that launched an AI task force, as well as a data center accountability plan, both intended to address, her office said, “growing concerns and risks posed by the rapid development of artificial intelligence — including workforce displacement, data privacy, and cybersecurity.”

Also on Friday, Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo, a Republican, signed an executive order that barred data centers from receiving a tax break on a particular school tax. His order also required data centers receiving other tax incentives from the state to cover their own power costs.

Less than 24 hours earlier, Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro, in an interview with NBC News,  called on the federal government to quickly pass regulations that would help rein in the AI industry — but also said he opposed pausing development on advanced AI models until those regulations were enacted.

“We’ve got to regulate this. We have to have real guardrails. We have to understand this technology better,” Shapiro told NBC News. “You’ve got to have third parties be in the rooms with these companies, understanding what they’re doing. When the CEO says, ‘I can’t control what I’ve built, and what I’m building could destroy humanity,’ that’s not time to kick the can down the road.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker — who, like Shapiro, are also thought to be mulling 2028 runs — have also called for action. Former President Barack Obama has also offered a warning, too, telling Democrats at a congressional campaign arm fundraiser that the party must have “a very clear plan” on AI policy and that he’d make it a central issue if he were running for president in 2028.

title: FBI warned immigration authorities about fake tradwife dating profiles
summary: An FBI memo said that a small group of women were posing with a “traditional wife” esthetic as a tactic to lure immigration authorities.
story: The FBI warned immigration officers internally that a group of women were creating fake online dating profiles with tradwife aesthetics to lure and dox them.

The FBI’s Chicago field office distributed a memo in February warning the country’s law enforcement agencies that a small group of women were creating the fake accounts in January targeting immigration authorities.
The dating profiles were “incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to an individuals in law enforcement,” according to the memo.

“The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online,” the memo reads. “The tactic is intended to generate public embarrassment and deter immigration enforcement activity.”

NBC News was provided the memo by Property of the People, a nonprofit organization focused on government transparency, which obtained it through a state open records request. The memo was first reported by The Guardian.
The FBI confirmed the authenticity of the memo to NBC News.

“While our standard practice is to not comment on specific intelligence products, the FBI regularly shares information with our law enforcement partners to assist in protecting the communities they serve as well as protecting those who serve and protect communities,” the agency said in a statement. “The FBI is committed to ensuring that law enforcement officers are safe from threats or violence while performing their duties.”
The memo did not state where the dating profiles were created or share examples of what the profiles contained.

It was sent amid a surge of thousands of immigration officers to the Twin Cities, dubbed by the federal government as “Operation Metro Surge.” The effort was ramped down after the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were protesting immigration enforcement in Minneapolis in January.
The immigration crackdown and killings prompted sweeping protests across the country and national furor against federal law enforcement.
The alleged dating profiles in Chicago were also created several months after an immigration enforcement surge there known as “Operation Midway Blitz.”

title: Watch How Amy Poehler Gets Famously Reserved Robert De Niro To Chit Chat More
summary: Leave it up to Amy Poehler to get a couple laughs out of one of the most iconically stoic actors of our day.
story: Leave it up to Amy Poehler to get a couple laughs out of one of the most iconically stoic actors of our day.

The “SNL” alum sat down with legendary actor Robert De Niro on the latest episode of her podcast “Good Hang,” released Sept. 15. While De Niro is famously known to be, well, not the chatterbox type, Poehler appears to get him to crack through a pretty nontraditional interview tactic.
“I’m gonna ask you a favor,” Poehler says, pleading with the actor. “If I don’t meet my word count by the end of this interview, I’m screwed.”
While De Niro seems to understand the assignment, he comes up a tad short when answering Poehler’s first question, “Would you consider yourself an introverted person?”
“In some ways I am,” he says. “Depending on the situation.”
And the comedian does not let him off the hook.
“We need at least 10,” Poehler replies, as the two dissolve into giggles. “We need at least 10 more words every sentence.”

During the podcast episode, Poehler and De Niro touch on a wide range of subjects from thirst traps to his new documentary “Tribeca 25,” which explores the beginnings of the famous film fest that he started with producer Jane Rosenthal after the 9/11 attacks.
The comedian truly hits it off with De Niro. At one point, she even moves him to tears when she praises his activism.
“It makes everybody feel very safe,” Poehler says of De Niro’s advocacy. “I’ve seen you do it over and over again, and I really appreciate it.”
Moments later, Poehler realizes that the comments have made De Niro emotional.
“This is going to be a real switcheroo,” Poehler says. “I can’t believe I just made you cry.”

title: Snooki Announces ‘Mawma Is Cancer Free’ After Diagnosis, Hysterectomy
summary: Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi announced in a Sept. 19 Instagram video that she is officially cancer-free.
story: Congratulations are in order!

Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi announced in a Sept. 19 Instagram video that she is officially cancer-free. The good news comes after the “Jersey Shore” star told fans in February that she was diagnosed with Stage 1 cervical cancer, undergoing a hysterectomy months later to treat the disease.
“After a colposcopy, conization & hysterectomy, mawma is cancer free,” Polizzi, 38, wrote in some text that accompanied a video of the reality star, enjoying a celebratory drink.
A colposcopy is a procedure that checks the cervix, vagina and vulva for signs of disease while conization refers to a different procedure in which abnormal tissue is removed from the cervix.
The announcement received an outpouring of support, including positive messages from fellow “Jersey Shore” cast mates Mike “The Situation” Sorrentino and Sammi “Sweetheart” Giancola.
Other social media users, who have also gone through cervical cancer, shared their excitement for Polizzi.

“I’m so happy for you and your family 🥹♥️ I know the struggle you have been through 🥹♥️I got diagnosed with cervix cancer in 2022 and went through chemo and radiation therapy, I’m cancer free now ♥️LOVE from Denmark ♥️” one user wrote.
In her post, Polizzi showed her appreciation for her medical team.
“Thanks to all the doctors who helped me on this journey!” Polizzi wrote in the caption. “It wouldn’t be possible without you!”
The reality star — who shared that she will be getting pap smears every three months to ensure that the disease doesn’t reappear — also encouraged women to be vigilant about their health.
“GET UR PAP SMEARS LADIES! & stay on top of those appointments!💗” Polizzi wrote.
Back in July, the mother of three shared a video on social media that gave fans a glimpse of her experience with hysterectomy surgery, documenting the entire day of the procedure.
“It’s a scary thing, and a lot of us women deal with it, and no one really talks about it,” Polizzi said in the video. “So I’m here to give that platform for all of us ladies.”

Polizzi also shared her honest emotions around the surgery. She said in the video that she was “terrified” while going into the procedure. The doctors ended up removing her uterus, cervix along with “some parts” of the vagina “just to make sure we get everything,” she said.
“Just dealing with all that pain — it’s not great,” a tearful Polizzi said.
