title: Did Lizzie Borden Ever Have A Romance With Maid Bridget Sullivan? An Expert Unpacks the True Story Behind ‘Monster’ Season 4
summary: Did Lizzie Borden have an affair with her maid? What historian Cara Robertson said in an interview.
story: In Netflix’s “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story,” domestic servant Bridget Sullivan is portrayed as a seductive manipulator who plays a substantial role in the dynamics that lead to Lizzie Borden’s infamous trial for the gruesome Aug. 1982 murders of her father and stepmother.
But the sensational nature of the series has viewers wondering if the maid, played by actor Vicky Krieps, was truly the figure who was stirring the pot in the real-life Borden family all along.

It turns out, the true story of Bridget Sullivan was far less salacious. And though the season, which was released on Sept. 17, depicts her as entangled in a romance with Lizzie Borden herself, experts and historical accounts show that the pair had a professional relationship — one that never crossed into the realm of lust.

As Cara Robertson — author of the book “The Trial of Lizzie Borden,” which is largely considered the definitive account of the case — tells TODAY.com, it “sounds as if they want to make this a sexy story and it just isn’t.”
How is Bridget Sullivan Portrayed in ‘Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story?’
Bridget makes her mark not long into the first episode of the series.

After the Borden household goes through a slew of maids, Bridget interviews with the family and immediately impresses matriarch Abby Borden, Lizzie’s harsh, hard-to-please stepmother, with the way in which she is able to remove a stubborn blood stain from a prized fainting couch. Patriarch Andrew Borden is also struck by Bridget’s presence, drawn to her lack of queasiness around blood — something that’s important to him as a woodworker who builds coffins for a living.

But perhaps the person most captivated by Bridget is Lizzie herself, particularly after the new maid takes a special interest in her, introducing Lizzie to some more risqué things, including a hand-cranked vibrator. Bridget also attempts to ingratiate herself with Lizzie but emphasizing Abby’s poor treatment of her.
“I don’t know why she belittles you like that,” Bridget says to Lizzie in the first episode, entitled “Bloodbath.” “She’s the most cruel woman I’ve ever seen.”
Though Lizzie appears to be more sympathetic to her stepmother’s temper, Bridget’s tactic works. And before long, there are secret bedroom visits and intimate meetings between the two.

Their sexual tension-filled bond is cemented by the end of the premiere episode when the two share a bath of cherry juice, inspired by Elizabeth Báthory, a 16th century Hungarian countess who is said to have bathed in the blood of young women to preserve her beauty, though Bathory’s infamous blood baths are likely myth rather than truth.
Earlier in the episode, it is Bridget who gifts the story of Báthory to Lizzie.
What Was The Real-Life Bridget Sullivan Really Like?
The real-life Bridget Sullivan was indeed a maid for the family. But aside from that detail, the similarities between Sullivan and her “Monster” character are few and far between.

Sullivan, who hailed from Ireland, worked for the Borden family for a number of years, starting in 1889, according to the Lizzie Borden House. However, according to Robertson’s book, she was not always happy with her employment, telling an officer that she had attempted to leave the position on multiple occasions.

As the book points out, most of the members of the Borden family did not bother to learn Sullivan’s name, calling her “Maggie,” simply because that was the name of the family’s domestic servant before her.
Sullivan also wasn’t particularly entrenched in the family’s drama, Robertson says.
“Bridget was an observer of the family tensions.  She lived in the house and negotiated the dynamics,” the author says.
Nor is there any evidence that Bridget was a master manipulator, she adds.

The 25-year-old Sullivan did end up becoming a key witness in the trial, as she was in the home at the time of the murders. Though Sullivan testified over the course of two days, she was ruled out as a possible suspect.
So Did Bridget Ever Have A Romance With Lizzie?

Over the decades, many have attempted to romantically link Lizzie Borden with Sullivan, especially because the former was never married and considered a spinster for the time. But the truth is that there’s just never been any evidence that points toward a steamy affair between the two. It was all just strictly professional, Robertson explains.

“This is simply a newer version of a longstanding desire to give Lizzie a fictional romance,” Robertson says. “It’s as if writers and adapters of the story can’t make their stories work without inserting a love interest.”
What’s more, the real-life Sullivan had a rather sunny view of Abby Borden. Robertson says that Abby Borden was the only person in the household who bothered to call her by her real name.
“We really don’t know much about her relationship with Abby,” Robertson says. “Bridget spoke positively of her after her death, calling her ‘a lovely woman.’”

Bridget Sullivan herself did eventually marry. After the murders, she eventually found her way to Anaconda, Montana where she tied the knot with laborer and fellow Irish immigrant John Sullivan, according to the Lizzie Borden House. With the middle-class living that John Sullivan was able to provide, Bridget Sullivan left behind her work as a domestic servant. She refused, however, to speak of the murders ever again.

title: ‘Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story’ Reviews: Here’s What Critics Are Saying
summary: “The Lizzie Borden Story,” the latest installment in Ryan Murphy’s “Monster” series is raising a few eyebrows. Find out if critics think it’s worth the watch.
story: Ryan Murphy has just released “The Lizzie Borden Story,” the latest installment in his “Monster” franchise.

Like past seasons, which include “The Jeffrey Dahmer Story,” “The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story” and “The Ed Gein Story,” Murphy’s latest offering is a true-crime horror series. This time it focuses on a century-old murder.

Starring Ella Beatty, Vicky Krieps, Rebecca Hall and Charlie Hunnam, the 8-episode series is based on the real-life killings of Abby and Andrew Borden. Residents of the Massachusetts city of Fall River, the Bordens were violently bludgeoned to death in their home in 1892, with each receiving multiple blows with a hatchet.

Their 32-year-old daughter, Lizzie, was arrested and charged in the crime. However, after a months’ long trial, Lizzie Borden was acquitted of the killings. While it’s been 134 years since the murders, it still remains one of the most famous unsolved crimes in American history.

Murphy, in collaboration with Ian Brennan and director Matt Winkler, brings the controversial crime story to the small screen in his newest Netflix series. And much like his previous offerings, “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story” has been met with both praise and pans.
If you’re wondering if the crime thriller is worth the watch, see below for a roundup of the latest reviews and decide for yourself.
Aramide Tinubu, TV critic, writes in Variety that the new series “has a playful, vibrant tone” and offers “something refreshing and wholly unique to the ‘Monster’ canon.”

Tinubu also writes that Murphy’s take on the Lizzie Borden story is a “highly watchable depiction of one of the most gruesome crimes in American history,” while acknowledging that the storyline “bends and twists the truth” of what actually transpired in 1892.
The Variety critic also writes that parts of the series highlight “the obsession with women’s appearances across time” in a way that adds to the show’s “fun campiness and gothic nature.”
She concludes that “The Lizzie Borden Story” is a reminder “that the last person anyone should underestimate is a woman, especially one clamoring for even a small slice of freedom.”
The Guardian
Lucy Mangan, TV critic, is less flattering in her write up for The Guardian, calling the latest “Monster” installment an “utterly bonkers, blood-soaked, borderline-fetishistic fever dream.”
In her review, Mangan likens the creative process behind the series to “the gleeful disgust of a roomful of adolescent boys being taught about the female reproductive system in PSHE.”

While the real-life Borden murders are a deeply complex mystery, The Guardian review suggests that “The Lizzie Borden Story” offers a much simpler message: “Women be crazy! Especially women who menstruate!”
Mangan does acknowledge that the show is stylish with a “Wes Anderson feel at times” and that it’s “full of great performances.”

But ultimately, Mangan writes that “The Lizzie Borden Story” feels as though it was created by “a bunch of boys on a dare who should have been called back after class and made to get down to some real work.”
The Hollywood Reporter
According to The Hollywood Reporter, the Lizzie Borden drama is nothing short of “faux-feminist nonsense.”

Television critic Angie Han writes that Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan desperately try to draw “anything meaningful out of Borden’s saga” and do so “with all the finesse of a college freshman trying to crank out a 15-page term paper in the two hours before deadline.”
Of actors Hall and Hunnam, Han writes, “There’s zero nuance to their performances, and also nothing unique about them to make them memorable.”

With the murder mystery seemingly solved early on in the series, Han writes that “The Lizzie Borden Story” struggles with “having eight hours’ worth of content to fill” and that the show “flails about for a number of stalling tactics, none of them particularly satisfying.”
The Wrap
“Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan have never been particularly interested in letting a little historical fact get in the way of a good story,” notes movie and TV critic Matthew Creith.

In his review for The Wrap, Creith writes that the creative team behind “The Lizzie Borden Story” takes one of America’s most infamous murder cases and “gleefully blends it into gothic horror, sexual melodrama and blood-soaked camp” and that the series is “hardly a conventional retelling of the Lizzie Borden case.”
So much so, Creith writes “calling it ‘The Lizzie Borden Story’ feels almost deliberately misleading.”
The “poisoned meals, bloody corpses, severed heads” and “axes flying around” make the show “frequently hilarious, even when it isn’t necessarily trying to be,” observes Creith.
Beyond that, he also faults “The Lizzie Borden Story” for randoming including the addition of real-life serial killer Aileen Wuornos “for absolutely no reason.”
Creith does, however, laud Sarah Paulson’s performance as Wuornos, calling it “manic, twitchy and unnerving and that it captures Wuornos “without making the character another true-crime caricature.”
He also notes Rebecca Hall’s “shrill, vicious” portrayal of Abby Borden, calling it a “scene-stealer” in the series.

In sum, “The Lizzie Borden Story” is one where “patriarchal cruelty meets female revenge, with history merely the jumping-off point,” he writes before concluding, “If that sounds like a mess … it is.”
Rotten Tomatoes
Finally, if you head over to Rotten Tomatoes, you’ll find that the series currently has a 50% on its “Tomatometer,” which averages critics’ reviews into a single median score.
On the site’s “Popcornmeter,” which measures audience reviews, “The Lizzie Borden Story” currently sits at 26%.

title: Who Is Rachel Danis? About Patrick Clancy’s Wife, Who Is Speaking Out in a New Interview
summary: Patrick Clancy and his wife Rachel Danis are speaking out following the conclusion of his ex-wife Lindsay Clancy’s triple murder trial, which ended in a mistrial.
story: Patrick Clancy and his wife Rachel Danis are speaking out following the conclusion of his ex-wife Lindsay Clancy’s triple murder trial, which ended in a mistrial. The two married after Patrick Clancy divorced Lindsay Clancy following the 2023 killings.
So who is Rachel Danis, the woman who is now Patrick Clancy’s new wife?

Danis sat down alongside Patrick Clancy for his pre-taped appearance on CBS’ “60 Minutes,” which will air on Sept. 20. The interview marks his first since a judge earlier this month declared a mistrial when a jury — who had been tasked with determining whether Lindsay Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three children — failed to reach a unanimous verdict.

During the trial, which ended Sept. 4, the prosecution argued that the mom had intentionally and knowingly attacked her children. Meanwhile, Lindsay Clancy’s defense did not dispute the fact that she had killed her children. But they argued that she is not criminally responsible for the murders, as she was consumed by the rare mental health condition postpartum psychosis.
Here’s what to know about Danis and her relationship with Patrick Clancy.
Who Is Rachel Danis?

Danis is a New York-based fertility doctor. According to her professional page, she’s specifically a reproductive endocrinologist and infertility specialist at clinic RMA of New York. She’s also an assistant clinical professor at Mount Sinai’s Icahn School of Medicine.

Danis specializes in endometriosis, an often painful condition in which tissue similar to what typically lines the uterus ends up on other organs. She also specializes in ovulation induction, LGBTQIA family building and fertility preservation, according to her professional biography. At one point, she was awarded a grant to conduct a clinical trial using Orlissa, a drug that aims to help patients manage moderate to severe endometriosis pain.

According to her professional bio, she’s somewhat of a fitness aficionado outside of work, and can often be found in a bootcamp class or ballet class. She also enjoys baking and strolls through Central Park, according to the website.
How Did She Meet Patrick Clancy?
Danis, who married Patrick Clancy in April, shared in a newly released clip from the upcoming “60 Minutes” interview that she met Clancy in Manhattan’s Central Park.
“I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday,” Danis said. “And I don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.”

Patrick Clancy, who divorced Lindsay Clancy following the 2023 killings, relocated to New York from the suburbs of Boston after the tragedy. By Oct. 2024, Clancy was living in what the New Yorker described in a feature as an apartment in Manhattan that resembled a “tidy bachelor pad,” which included a few keepsakes from his late children Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. Clancy did not comment on his relationship status with Lindsay Clancy at the time, nor did he mention Danis.
Lindsay Clancy’s defense attorney Kevin Reddington confirmed in court that Patrick Clancy had remarried and is “trying to move on.”
How Was Danis Impacted During The Trial?

While Danis did not take the stand during the nearly six-week trial over the summer, Patrick Clancy spent two days testifying on the events that led up to the killings in addition to Lindsay Clancy’s deteriorating mental health prior to the tragedy.

However Danis became a topic of conversation when conspiracies began to arise on social media from internet users who accused Patrick Clancy of killing his children. Others online have also accused the father of framing the defendant. And in the days that followed the trial, Danis and Patrick Clancy were frequently the subject of paparazzi photos in addition to harassment.
In the upcoming interview, Danis defends their marriage.

“I don’t understand how the story has been so twisted, but I would hope people know that Pat is, as I said before, the most selfless father and supportive partner,” she said in the newly released clip.

Patrick Clancy and others involved in the case have made multiple attempts to shut down internet conspiracies. In a Sept. 9 interview with NBC News’ Laura Jarrett, Reddington called on people to stop spreading misinformation and attacking Patrick Clancy.
“His life has been turned upside down into a nightmare that he doesn’t deserve,” Reddington said. “Period. Full stop.”
The defense attorney added that he has “said it repeatedly, unequivocally, that there is absolutely no way that this guy deserves what he has been living (through).”

The day prior, Patrick Clancy’s attorneys also attempted to shut down the noise from conspiracy theorists. One of his attorneys, Howard Cooper, mentioned in a statement that law enforcement “has been notified” about the claims and that “every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally.”
“This campaign, now fueled by insatiable media coverage, remains at a fever pitch and has resulted in real life threats to his reputation, livelihood, and life,” Cooper said in the Sept. 8 statement.

title: Lucy Foley Revives Agatha Christie’s Miss Marple For the Character’s First Novel in 50 Years. Read the Prologue
summary: Sleuth Miss Marple, created by Agatha Christie, has once again found herself at the scene of a crime in Lucy Foley’s “Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel.” Read the prologue.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.
After 50 years away, cunning and perceptive sleuth Miss Marple has once again found herself at the scene of a crime.

The elderly character at the center of many Agatha Christie whodunits is tasked with solving a new case in Lucy Foley’s latest mystery “Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel,” out Sept. 22. Christie is also listed as an author.

Set at a secluded resort in Switzerland, the Grand Alpine is practically cut off from the outside world, only accessible via a gondola ride during particular hours of the day. And it’s precisely there that the book begins. The prologue opens with the line:
The gondola rises silently through the bank of clouds into the frozen world at the top of the mountain.

Foley tells TODAY.com the eerie, chilling setting was the perfect place to make Miss Marple — who last appeared in a novel in Christie’s 1976 work “Sleeping Murder” — the “beating heart” of the story.

The bestselling British author behind “The Guest List” and “The Paris Apartment” grew up a fan of Christie, discovering one of her detective novels on a bookshelf in a cottage when she was just 12. She devoured more stories but she didn’t appreciate Miss Marple’s character, she recalls.
It wasn’t until she re-read some of Christie’s novels that she admired how the writer took an “underdog character” and made “her a master sleuth with a brain to rival Sherlock Holmes.”

“It was so clever, and it still feels radical even today,” Foley says. “I think we still have an issue with older women being perceived as invisible or less capable in some way. I still think she has something to teach us.”

In 2022, Foley was asked to contribute to a collection of 12 new Marple stories, alongside Leigh Bardugo, Ruth Ware, Jean Kwok and more. When she was approached again about the character, this time for a full-length novel, she jumped at the opportunity.

“In 2026, we need a new kind of superhero. We’re surrounded by these male egos and these men rewriting history to further their own ends. I love thinking, ‘What would Miss Marple make of them, and how would she thwart them?’” she says.

Still, she initially felt the pressure of doing the character justice. But once she had her premise — Miss Marple on a holiday to the Swiss Alps in the 1950s — she entered her creative bubble and started plotting the mystery.

“It felt like quite a haunted time in many ways because there was this long shadow of the Second World War. I wanted that to be something that I contrasted with the glamour,” she says of the setting of “Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel.”

She also knew how she wanted to structure the novel. Fans of Foley’s other books will know that the writer tells each chapter from a different character’s first person point of view. With Miss Marple, though, she decided readers wouldn’t hear the inner workings of the detective’s mind.

“I knew that I couldn’t have her perspective because that would feel like a real Christie anachronism,” she says, laughing. “Because I think the really interesting thing about Miss Marple is she’s quite enigmatic, and she doesn’t actually necessarily reveal a lot of herself.”

The character works best as an underestimated observer, Foley shares, and she wanted to keep her that way. She read, and re-read, Christie’s books to nail Miss Marple’s tone and mannerisms. She also watched the British television series.

“There were two things that I knew I had to get right for this book before I brought in any of my own sort of creative sensibilities, and those were the Christie plotting… (and) also Miss Marple. So I wanted to get her on the page as closely as I possibly could to Christie’s Miss Marple,” Foley says.
Beyond that, she says she had “some license” to bring in her own voice and style.
“I wanted it to be a book that was in conversation with the original Miss Marple,” Foley says. “They didn’t want to present it as a kind of Agatha Christie forgery.”
With those goals in mind, Foley plotted out the entire book before she started writing, a change to her usual process.

While Miss Marple isn’t mentioned in the prologue, she is quickly introduced in Chapter 1, which is told from the perspective of Diana Glass, described as “the help.” Diana meets Miss Marple and describes her as a “the perfect image of a little old lady — almost too perfect, in fact.”

“I wanted, through Diana’s eyes, a reader who’s familiar with Miss Marple to recognize this character that they know and love. But also a reader coming to her completely cold, not knowing much about her, to quite quickly get a sense of who she is through Diana’s perspective,” Foley says.
Readers then meet more characters who will all become suspects in the death of the unnamed person found in the gondola. Miss Marple must suss out the culprit before they commit their next crime.

“As a reader of murder mysteries, I love this sense of the past catching up with people and people not getting away with things when they shouldn’t,” Foley says. “But I also love this idea, chaos is then going to be resolved for you at the end. There’s a nice wrapping up and a nice sense of resolution. I think that can be quite soothing and satisfying in troubled times.”
It’s all set up in a prologue, which Foley says was the first scene she thought of when she started writing.
“The first scene that came to me was the gondola going up the mountain,” she says. “The set piece of someone getting into the gondola alive and well at the bottom, and being found dead at the top.”
Get a taste of the mystery below.
Read the Prologue of Lucy Foley’s ‘Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel’
The top of the Grand Alpine gondola
Swiss Alps, 1950

The gondola rises silently through the bank of clouds into the frozen world at the top of the mountain. It is a wonder of modern engineer-ing, gliding between stanchions drilled into ancient rock, the red lacquer of its body gaudy against the bleak palette of white and gray.

There’s someone in the gondola. One of the hotel guests, most likely, eager to make the first tracks of the day. Fresh snow fell last night, leaving a pristine covering of powder over the mountain and softening the glacier that sweeps down one side. In the early morning light, it gives off a nacreous glow. Faint bluish indentations on the surface whisper of hidden, lethal chasms beneath.

In the tiny cabin beside the lift the attendant stamps his feet in his boots, blows on his hands to keep warm. He’s looking forward to interacting with another human being, however briefly. It’s a lonely existence up here with only the eagles for company, the only sounds the otherworldly groaning and cracking of the glacial ice as it con-tinues its endless creep toward the town. He knows the fears of his ancestors, how they believed in malign mountain spirits and giants living among these peaks, why they shunned them as a place of dark magic. Sometimes—­ when the seracs fall with crashes that seem to echo infinitely among the surrounding rock, or when a winter storm crackles with purple lightning, or when the low growl of an avalanche sounds at a distance—­ he’s not completely sure he doesn’t believe in such things himself.

The shadowy figure in the gondola sits with their head thrown back against the rear window; perhaps in awestruck appreciation of the view. The mechanism grinds to a halt. The doors begin to open. The seated figure does not move.

The attendant peers through the cabin window. Are they asleep? Are they not intending to get out? Perhaps they’ve come up here for the sights and will simply stay put and travel back the way they’ve come. More snow is on the way, after all: a great deal of it.
And yet . . . there’s something odd. A peculiar stillness about the scene. The attendant feels that he is just as alone as he was before the gondola and its occupant emerged through the clouds.
Should he go and see?
He doesn’t want to see.
He’s struck by the sudden impulse (odd; he’s a good Swiss Prot-estant) to cross himself.

Just as he steps out of his cabin into the freezing air the gondola gives the mechanical shudder that locks it into the final position. This is when the seated figure falls, stiff and inert as a Dresden doll knocked from a mantelpiece, keeling face-­ first onto the metal floor of the cabin.
For a moment the attendant watches in horror. Then he springs into action. But he knows, even as he hastens along the ice-­ slick path, that it is no use. The gondola’s passenger is already dead.

title: ‘The Traitors’ Cast Just Dropped, and it Features a ‘Love Island’ Narrator, a Former ‘Bachelor’ and Glinda the Good Witch
summary: Who is in the cast of The Traitors season 5? Read on for a full list and where you know them from.

title: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson on How that ‘Brothers’ Rumor Came to Be
summary: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson explain how the rumor that they are brothers came to be, why McConaughey won’t take a DNA test, and more.
story: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson have been such good friends for so long, it’s almost like they’re brothers.
Their 30-year friendship, Texas roots and nine-year age difference have birthed a tantalizing rumor: Are they actually related?

The Oscar-winning McConaughey, 56, and the Emmy-winning Harrelson, 65, have fun with that notion in their new Apple TV series “Brothers,” which premieres on Sept. 23 and is loosely inspired by their own story.
While they’ve enjoyed playing with what their new show calls a “true rumor,” they told Craig Melvin on his “Glass Half Full” podcast that it’s not inconceivable they could be related.
In an excerpt of their conversation that aired on TODAY Sept. 18, McConaughey recalled how the conversation of them possibly being brothers originated.

“One night on a family vacation about nine years ago, we’re all together and that little lingo’s going back and forth: ‘Man, it’s like, look at y’all, y’all’s mannerisms and you look...’ and da da da da,” McConaughey said.
McConaughey said his mother, Mary Kathleen “Kay” McConaughey, now 94, was on “her third Kendall-Jackson” wine when she surprised her son and Harrelson with some news.
“Well, she leaned over and said, ‘I knew ... your father,’” Harrelson said. “I’m, like, first of all, that ellipsis was long.”
“Even my 6-year-old son got the innuendo of that ellipsis,” McConaughey said.
“They must’ve done a little bit,” Harrelson said.
The revelation had the family buzzing.

“And so all the kids started going, like ‘Oooh,’ running around and going, like, ‘ahhhh,’” McConaughey said. “The kids start pulling out pictures so we can do a timeline. They find out that actually when it would have happened/could have happened, was actually during my mom and dad’s second divorce.”
Kay McConaughey and Matthew’s father, Jim, divorced each other twice and married each other three times during their 24-year relationship.
“And so possibly this fits the timeline that would’ve been out of wedlock in the second divorce when she might’ve made a little trip for dalliance,” McConaughey surmised.
“And they just both happened to be in the same area, and, you know, she’s not an unattractive woman, even now,” Harrelson said while laughing.
“She’s not an unattractive woman,” McConaughey echoed.
“Yeah, and this was when she’s in her 20s, was it?” Harrelson asked.
“His dad was available,” McConaughey said.
It makes sense to the two actors. Harrelson joked that it’s like a line in a song.
“Mom was hot...” McConaughey said.
“...And my dad was available,” they both joked.
The new Apple show, which marks their first time as co-stars since the first season of HBO’s “True Detective” in 2014, is a fictionalized look at their possible family ties.

“We are playing ourselves, but we’re playing sort of heightened versions on what we’re kind of stereotyped as,” McConaughey said. “We play a little parody of ourselves, and our friendship’s been going on for 30-something years.”
Harrelson tries to find out the truth to the rumor through a DNA test on the show, but McConaughey doesn’t want to do it. That plotline mirrors real life.
“It’s not true,” McConaughey said. “I don’t believe it’s true anyway.”

“He doesn’t want it to be true, because he doesn’t want to lose a father, but he doesn’t realize he gains a father that he never met,” Harrelson said. “It’s a net gain because he gets an extra brother from me.”

Regardless of whether they share the same blood, they are as close as brothers. They presented at the Emmy Awards on Sept. 14, took in the sensational comeback win by McConaughey’s beloved University of Texas football team over Ohio State on Sept. 12, and were seen together at the U.S. Open in New York City a week earlier.
Sometimes the relationship almost gets a little too comfortable.
“This man has never gone through a front door in his life,” McConaughey said. “He’s never called or sent a message from anyone to say, ‘Hey, it’s been a year, but I’m coming over.’”
“The Last Bus” star recalled a time he was living with his wife, Camila Alves, and children in Los Angeles and Harrelson decided to drop by in the most unexpected way possible.
“Two in the morning, wake up. What is in between us in bed?” McConaughey said. “He had jumped the fence, picked the window, snuck in and got in bed with us.”
“What a good way to wake up a friend,” Harrelson said. “You know what I mean? And get to be next to Camila. That was nice. She was warm to me.”
Just another wild moment in a friendship full of them.
“You think he’s staying for the weekend, then it’s three months later,” McConaughey said.

title: Rebecca Ross Reveals Cover of New Romantic Fantasy, ‘A Bittersweet Spell’
summary: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.

Rebecca Ross keeps a brainstorming journal. In it are snippets of sentences, flashes of characters, ideas for structures, and, first written in 2023, what ended up being the first line of the first book of her first trilogy.
Of course he traveled to the edge of the realm to find her."
This sentence opens Chapter 1 of Ross’ “A Bittersweet Spell,” set for release on April 6, 2027.

“Sometimes I feel like you don’t know how to write the first chapter until you’ve written the last chapter,” Ross says. “But that line was just so strong to me that it has been there since the first draft.”

Ross revealed the novel’s cover and shared the first few paragraphs exclusively with TODAY.com, previewing her new adult romantic fantasy centering on two people forced to reunite 10 years after a betrayal to translate a magical manuscript.

Ross recalls that right after she wrote that first sentence in her journal, she found a character with a “strong voice,” the perfect vessel to pursue a bigger writing goal she had set for herself: writing a story within a story.
Ross, who rose to prominence with the BookTok darling “Divine Rivals” duology, says the concept of writing a frame narrative has long been “marinating in my imagination.”
“I was waiting for the right characters to come along, waiting for really, the right setting and plot,” she says.

Then she met Lorne, the character readers meet at the start of the novel. She continued writing in his voice and “knew right away that I was dealing with two characters that had previous history that didn’t end very well, and yet he still needs her again.”
Readers meet Lorne — and learn of Avalene, the “one that got away for him” — as follows:

Of course, he traveled to the edge of the realm to find her. But if Lorne remembered anything about Avalene Vale, it was this: She preferred gloomy days, bittersweet endings, and drank tea when the sun set. Most of all, she was the only paleographer Lorne knew of who was also an illuminer; she could read enchanted ink.

That troublesome ink was why he now stood atop salt- streaked cliffs with a leather folder tucked beneath his arm, staring at a cottage that was built on the brink of the kingdom. A stone house with a thatched roof and stained glass windows that overlooked the sprawl of ocean. A forlorn sort of place that Lorne would have passed by had the fisherman not mentioned the woman who dwelled here had strange eyes. One dark blue, like the sky at eventide, and one a few shades lighter. The color of the sea just after a thunderstorm.

Lorne wanted nothing more than to forget those uncanny eyes of hers, and he had been successful for the past decade. Avalene had lived in only the darkest regions of his mind, a hum of static that found its flesh in the occasional dream. But now he needed her, and how that need galled him. The gods must be laughing at him.

Chapter 1 immediately sets the stage for the two stories at the heart of “A Bittersweet Spell”: There’s Lorne and Avalene’s reunion and the story contained in the enchanted manuscript that only together they can transcribe.
“I knew as I was writing, I was like ‘Oh, there’s so much stuff here. there’s so much material that I know I’m going to need multiple books,’” Ross says.

“A Bittersweet Spell” will be the first book of Ross’ first trilogy. Book 1 will start with Lorne’s point of view and slowly introduce Avalene’s perspective as well, with their chapters written in third person. As they translate the manuscript, readers will also learn the story of Faye, a nun, mage and scribe.

“It makes for I think, as far as a reader going into it, it’s a very rich type of experience, where you’re going to be taking in different documents and beginning to put all the pieces together because the plot is very intricate,” Ross says.
“There’s certain moments that I feel like as a reader gets through the book, you start seeing how everything connects,” she adds.

title: Who Survived the First Night in ‘The Traitors: New Blood’ Series Premiere?
summary: “The Traitors: New Blood” kicked off with plenty of twists. Here’s what happened in Episodes 1 and 2, including who was murdered and banished.
story: The premiere of “The Traitors: New Blood” introduced 22 reality television newbies ready to take over Alan Cumming’s cutthroat game.

The all-civilian version of the Emmy-winning series arrived on NBC Thursday, Sept. 17, with a supersized two-hour episode. In the premiere, viewers briefly met the 22 contestants as they boarded a train and made their way to the castle, located in the Scottish Highlands.
There, they only had a few moments to get acquainted and tell a couple lies before some of them were secretly selected to be murderous Traitors.
“A new dawn is rising. But make no mistake, you are not in Kansas anymore,” Alan warned them.

He then revealed new twists that will shake up the game. By the end of the episode, two contestants had already been eliminated and a covert mission was underway. Read on for a recap of the first two episodes of “The Traitors: New Blood.”
The Traitors Are Selected

After the contestants arrived at the castle, Alan shared the first of many new elements added to the game for the all-civilian season. He announced that as an “extra incentive” $15,000 will be added to the prize pot this season every time the Faithfuls successfully banish a Traitor.

But who are the Traitors? Well, fans didn’t have to wait long for Alan to choose the players who will have to murder their fellow contestants every night. As soon as the players moved into the castle, they joined him at the Round Table. They donned blindfolds while Alan quietly tapped the shoulders of the Traitors: funeral director Joe and pilot Tomica.
While he didn’t share with the group how many Traitors he chose, he did confirm the selection wasn’t complete. Alan said an additional player would be chosen soon.
First Mission

The players’ strength and endurance skills were put to the test in the first mission of the season. The players had to locate three crates in the loch that were filled with treasure chests, each worth $10,000. Then, they would use the numbers on the crates to find a code for a captain’s safe, giving them an additional $20,000.
While completing the mission, the players also had an opportunity to grab one of three available shields.
They finished the mission before time ran out, adding $50,000 to the prize pot. Victor, Abby L and Madeline secured shields.
The Traitors Meet in the Turret
Before learning the other’s identity, each traitor separately met with Alan and he handed them their cloak. They were asked to recite the Traitor’s Oath before entering the turret.

Joe and Tomica removed their cloaks and met for the first time as Traitors. They quickly celebrated before Alan interrupted to share another twist: they must select two Faithfuls to become their “accomplices.”

“For the next 24 hours, they will be put through a series of tests to see if they have what it takes to impress you as a Traitor. And at the end of that period, you will select one of them to join your treacherous ranks. As for the other, they will face the cruelest of cuts as you will murder them!” Alan explained.
The episode ended with two masked accomplices meeting in the woods.
Who Are the Accomplices?
The second episode opened with the accomplices learning about their head-to-head battle. They removed their masks, revealing that Katie and Xavier were chosen by the Traitors.
We then returned to the turret, where Tomica and Joe were discussing their shortlist for murder. They named Michael, Kim and Arisa as their three options.
Back in the woods, Xavier and Katie murdered one of the three by sailing them down a river in a coffin.
Who Was Murdered First?
At the first breakfast of the season, the contestants arrived in groups. It was confirmed that Kim, a lawyer who was masquerading as a college basketball coach to deceive the cast, was murdered.
“I’m pissed. I wish I could’ve lasted beyond today. But Traitors, maybe you made a smart decision. Because I was going to find out who you were,” Kim said before departing.
The First Round Table Banishment
The surprises kept coming as Alan strolled into the breakfast room and shared that the first Round Table would commence shortly.

The players only had minutes to check in with each other, and some didn’t use their time wisely. While speaking with Victor and Kriste, Madeline said “I’d feel like s--- picking Kim” to be murdered. But Kriste misheard her, thinking Madeline admitted she murdered Kim. Kriste retold the conversation to multiple players before the Round Table.
Meanwhile, Xavier and Katie were both trying to prove their worth to the Traitors. Xavier decided his best strategy was to make Katie appear suspicious.
At the Round Table, Victor instantly became a target. Many players called him out for focusing on the shield as soon as the mission started, indicating he wasn’t a “team player.”
Kriste then mentioned her conversation with Madeline, who denied making the comment about Kim. The two shared a heated exchange. “I know that you’re bald-face lying,” Kriste told Madeline.
Kriste convinced most of the cast to vote for Madeline and she was banished.
While standing on the Circle of Truth, Madeline said before leaving, “Kriste is a liar. I never said that. I am a Faithful.”
The Accomplices’ Test

After the Round Table, Xavier and Katie separately received notes about a task they needed to complete. The letter explained that there were two blank death warrants hidden in the castle, one in the library and another in the atrium. Xavier and Katie had until the clock chimed to retrieve the warrants and deliver them to the Traitors.
“Remember, the Traitors are watching,” the note said.
The episode ended on a cliffhanger, with both Xavier and Katie attempting to grab the warrants and avoid suspicion.
What Will Happen Next Week?
“The Traitors: New Blood” returns Thursday, Sept. 24, for another extended episode. Next week, fans will find out if Xavier and Katie completed their test and which one the Traitors recruited.
Episodes 3 and 4 will air at 8 p.m. ET/PT on NBC.

title: Miley Cyrus Shares Details of Final Conversation with Dolly Parton in New Interview
summary: Miley Cyrus is revealing a few details about the last conversation she had with her godmother Dolly Parton, who died in August.
story: Miley Cyrus is revealing a few details about the last conversation she had with her godmother Dolly Parton, who died in August.

Cyrus opened up about her relationship with Parton amid a Sept. 17 interview with Apple Music’s Zane Lowe. During their chat, Cyrus spoke about a tradition she’s had with Parton since she started to release music on vinyl.

“Dolly has been the first person that when I get a vinyl printed, that’s the first person I send it to since I’ve been making vinyls, and this time around I’m going to send her a vinyl because I always do,” she said about her plans for new album, “Bass Persuades,” out Sept. 18.
“But the time that we talked, which was the last time we would talk, it was actually me telling her about this record,” she continued as she became emotional.

Parton, who died at age 80, has long been a critical part of Miley Cyrus’ life. The “Jolene” singer toured with, and became close to, Miley Cyrus’ father, fellow country singer Billy Ray Cyrus. And she assumed the role of godmother upon Miley Cyrus’ birth in 1992.
Over the years, Parton collaborated with Miley Cyrus on music, performing together several times. She also guest starred in three episodes of Miley Cyrus’ Disney Channel show “Hannah Montana.”
In the Apple Music interview, the “Flowers” singer said that even though the she and Parton were so different, they perfectly matched one another.

“She knew this and I know this, she is known for the faux, the fake, the hair, the makeup, the show of it,” Cyrus explained. “But there’s a part of her that’s what I think everyone gravitates towards, (which) is how real she is and how authentic she is.”
She said it was one of the many ways she related to Parton. And it became particularly apparent as she began her career singing as her alter ego “Hannah Montana.”

“I think a way that I could look at that as you can have a persona and still be who you are is because I had Dolly,” she shared. “Sometimes I call what I do drag because the way that I present myself is just someone that is so different from the person that feeds the tortoise every morning. But again, that person’s inside of me. I just kind of have her off.”
The Grammy winner then shared more about her connection with Parton. She said she would frequently call the “9 to 5” singer for advice, asking “‘What do I do now?’”
Parton always gave her the best responses, of course.

“She was always right,” Cyrus said. “It’s like how your mom’s always right, and when you’re a kid, you’re like, ‘What does she know?’ And then as you get older, you’re like, ‘Everything. How? Where did this come from? You’re just a normal person. Why do you know everything?’ Dolly was just always right about stuff.”
She also revealed Parton was the one who encouraged her to wear a Bob Mackie dress for her 2024 Grammys performance. She sported a voluminous ‘do Parton would approve of that night, too.
“I would’ve never worn Bob Mackie if it wasn’t for Dolly…she was like, ‘You need to just fake it.’”
The interview comes after Cyrus paid tribute to her “fairy godmother” in a sweet Instagram post Aug. 26.

Alongside a black-and-white photo of Parton, she wrote, “The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts.”
She added that she was sure Parton would want her to sing about how she was feeling. She also said she knows that despite the loss, she will always have “an angel” by her side.

“I will always love her and want to make her proud,” Cyrus wrote. “My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things.”

title: Mane Makeover! Mom of 2 Gets Her Waist-Length Hair Cut Into a Bixie, Sees the Results for the First Time Live on Air
summary: Sometimes, a haircut is all it takes to get out of a funk and feel fresh — especially if your hairstylist is responsible for Jennifer Aniston’s ’90s looks on “Friends.”
story: Sometimes, a haircut is all it takes to get out of a funk and feel fresh — especially if your hairstylist is responsible for Jennifer Aniston’s ’90s looks on “Friends.”
For Pritsana, one of TODAY’s guests on the Sept. 17 show, her transformation called for chopping off an entire ponytail.

In the Mane Makeover segment, Jenna Bush Hager and Sheinelle Jones bring in esteemed celebrity stylists to give TODAY fans the change they’ve been craving. Studio 1A welcomed back Chris McMillan, a celebrity hairstylist, who gave two viewers completely new ‘dos. And this time, there was a special twist: The guests saw their makeover results for the first time live on TODAY.
To pull it off, the TODAY crew covered nearby mirrors, and Jenna and Sheinelle couldn’t see the monitors during the broadcast. This also means McMillan did 100% of the cuts without a mirror.
Here are the results.
Pritsana
As a mom of two, caregiver to her parents and a design business owner, this New Yorker, like many, finds herself with little time for glamour.

Pritsana said on TODAY she regularly made hair appointments but would have to reschedule or cancel altogether. The length of her hair had grown out of control, and she hadn’t had a proper haircut in two years.
With her makeover, she wanted a lighter, more polished cut that helps manage the change in texture she’s noticed as she’s entered her late 40s.
Ready for a dramatic change, Pritsana got what she wished for with this real-time reveal.
“Oh, I love it! I love it!” Pritsana said after a gasp.
